Jñāna Yoga for Anxiety

A practical guide · free to read

Jñāna Yoga for Anxiety

A practical guide to living with anxiety, built as one long illustrated scroll. Real stories, the science in plain words, and the tools that got me through, in fourteen chapters you can read straight through or dip into whenever you need one. It's free, for anyone who is suffering. Along the way I quote the teachers who helped me, some of them at length, and wherever I do I link to their work on Spotify, Amazon and Audible so you can go to the source.

One of the best tools for a panic attack is the 5-4-3-2-1 method, so it's built into every page. The button in the corner is always there. Tap it and it walks you through naming five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell and one you can taste. About two minutes, and your attention is out of the loop and back in the room.

A note before you begin. This book shares one person's experience and the practices that helped him. It is not medical advice and does not replace care from a doctor or a mental health professional. If you are in crisis, call or text 9-8-8 (Canada and the US, any time). In an emergency, call 911.

Chapter 1

I've Been Down Here Before

Before the maps and the methods, a word about who's handing them to you, and where this book is going.

I've Been Down Here Before1 / 11

A guy falls in a hole.

The walls are too steep to climb. A doctor walks by, and the guy shouts up for help. The doctor writes a prescription, drops it in the hole and keeps walking. A priest comes by. He writes out a prayer, drops it in and keeps walking.

Then a friend comes by, and he jumps in. The guy says, are you crazy? Now we're both stuck down here. And the friend says,

"Yeah, but I've been down here before, and I know the way out."

Leo McGarry tells this story to Josh Lyman in The West Wing, "Noël" (season 2, 2000), teleplay by Aaron Sorkin. Leo is a recovering alcoholic. Josh is struggling after being shot.

That's the only qualification I have.

I've Been Down Here Before2 / 11

I had anxiety for 35 years before I knew what it was called.

I had panic attacks, usually during kidney stones. For a long stretch I threw up before work most days. The rest is on the map, and the map isn't complete.

I was lost in thought, stuck in a dark state, for a very long time. I'd become a machine that ran on old trauma and reacted the same way to everything.

Nobody told me the body had to settle before the mind could. So I went straight at the thoughts and lost, for years. That's why this book doesn't start with thoughts.

I've had enough trauma to make a room full of people cry. I've worked through it, and I'm at peace with it. I'll assume you've had your share too, and I'll go gently.

I've Been Down Here Before3 / 11

I thought the next win would fix it. It never did.

So I chased the next thing. If I just had this, or just had that, it would all be okay. Sometimes it was, for a moment.

But I checked nearly everything off my list, and none of it touched the anxiety. Each win felt like one more weight to carry.

Success doesn't end suffering. It gives you more to suffer about.

My mind was my master. Now it's my tool.

I've Been Down Here Before4 / 11

At 39, a song opened a door.

I'd started swapping the content that fed my dark moods for playlists that were calm or upbeat. In 2019 the composer East Forest put out an album with Ram Dass, and the algorithm served me one track, "I Am Loving Awareness."

I'd tried every kind of meditation and every way to get healthier, and nothing had stuck. But about a month into this one phrase, the load started to lift. My shoulders came down from around my ears. The tight chest and the daily nausea eased.

An old man who seemed to love his wheelchair was telling me to love everybody. Even my dark thoughts.

Who is this guy?

The album is Ram Dass by East Forest (2019), built from teachings recorded in Ram Dass's study on Maui. Krishna Das sings on "I Am Loving Awareness."

I've Been Down Here Before5 / 11

A companion

Ram Dass

1931–2019

  • HarvardBorn Richard Alpert, he became a psychology professor. He and Timothy Leary researched psychedelics until Harvard dismissed them both in 1963.
  • India, 1967He met Neem Karoli Baba, known as Maharaj-ji, who named him Ram Dass, "servant of God." Be Here Now followed in 1971.
  • Vancouver, 1969He gave the talks released as Here We All Are. I've played them so many times I could almost recite them.
  • A stroke, 1997It slowed his speech and put him in a wheelchair. He came to call it a gift.
  • Maui, 2019He died at 88, the same year his voice reached me.

I'm a logical, scientific guy. My younger self would have been put off by all the spirituality. But you get to test this for yourself. It works for you or it doesn't. I felt freer than I had in years.

Be Here NowRam DassBook ↗
I've Been Down Here Before6 / 11

Jñāna means knowing. Not the kind you can look up.

It's Sanskrit for knowledge or wisdom, from the same ancient root as the Greek gnosis and the English know. But the knowing it points to happens somewhere other than the thinking mind. You can read every book about swimming and still drown. Jñāna is the knowing you have once you've been in the water.

The Indian mystic Ramakrishna drew the line with fire.

One who has merely heard of fire has ajñāna, ignorance. One who has seen fire has jñāna, knowledge. One who has built a fire and cooked on it has vijñāna, realization.Sri Ramakrishna, as the teaching is usually retold

Most of us have only heard of peace. This book is about seeing it, and then cooking on it.

Jñāna yoga is the mind beating out the mind.

That's the whole method in one line. You use the thinking mind to look closely at the thinking mind, until it sees through its own tricks. The anxious thoughts don't get argued with. They get seen for what they are, and they lose their grip.

The fire version is how the teaching is usually retold. In The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna he makes the point with milk (heard of it, seen it, drunk it) and with fire hidden in wood, which you first know is there and then cook rice on.

The Gospel of Sri RamakrishnaMahendranath GuptaBook ↗Audiobook ↗
I've Been Down Here Before7 / 11

Three paths up the same mountain. This book takes the path of knowing.

The Bhagavad Gita, one of yoga's oldest and most loved texts, lays out three paths to the same summit. They suit different kinds of people, and most of us walk a bit of each.

Jñāna yoga is the path of knowledge. You look closely at your own mind and ask what's really true, until the false ideas fall away. It suits the person who can't stop asking why. The everyday version is catching a scary thought mid-flight and asking, is that so?

Karma yoga is the path of action. You do the work in front of you, do it well, and let go of how it turns out. It suits the doer, the one who feels better after a day of honest work than after a day of talk. The everyday version is washing the dishes without keeping score.

Bhakti yoga is the path of love and devotion. You pour your heart into something greater than yourself, whether that's God, a guru, or everyone you meet. It suits the person who feels first and thinks second. The everyday version is a kitchen full of singing, or a prayer before bed.

This book walks the path of knowledge, because an anxious mind is already a thinking mind. It's driving the wrong way down a one-way street, and I'd rather turn it around than tell it to stop thinking. The other two paths show up anyway. Chapter 13 is karma yoga. Ram Dass, the companion you've just met, walked mostly on bhakti, with his heart given to his guru.

Teachers rarely start a student on jñāna. The usual road settles the body first, because a mind that's on fire can't look at itself. I'm going to borrow that part of the road. The next three chapters are the Basics: what the alarm is, the levers that calm it, and the breath. They're the ground everything else stands on. Then we turn the mind around.

There are a thousand paths to the same place, and each of us walks our own. This book is the map and the methods I found on mine.

Ramakrishna's chief disciple, Swami Vivekananda, carried these paths to the West, starting at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago. He taught a fourth alongside them: raja yoga, the path of meditation, which is Patanjali's eight limbs. Chapter 11 walks through its last four steps.

I've Been Down Here Before8 / 11

Four things I hope you'll walk away with

Understand it.A new way of seeing anxiety, and tools, tricks and tips for managing it every day.
Settle.If you're living in sensitization, a way out of it, and out of the worry about worry.
Be here.More of your life lived in the present moment, as a practice takes root.
See who you are.If you're ready to hear it. This one can change how you see almost everything.

Understanding it is the minimum. Seeing who you are is a bonus, and you can only hear it once you're the one asking the question. If it doesn't land yet, call it a seed for another day.

The book moves in that order, too. The first movement settles the body: the Basics. The second watches the mind. The third asks where you begin and end. The fourth comes back down the mountain to live here, win or lose, dishes and all.

I've Been Down Here Before9 / 11

Before we start

Take what helps. Leave the rest.

I'm not a doctor, a therapist or a psychologist. Nothing in this book replaces real medical care. If something in your body worries you, get it checked.

Some of what's coming will shake ideas you've carried a long time. If a page unsettles you, skip it, or put the book down for a while. I won't be offended.

And if anxiety spikes while you read, there's a button in the corner of every page marked 5·4·3·2·1. It opens a two-minute grounding exercise: you name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell and one you can taste. Panic lives in a loop of thought. The senses only work in the present, so naming what they find pulls you out of the loop and back into the room. Chapter 2 teaches it properly. Until then, it's there whenever you need it.

Yoga comes from Sanātana Dharma, the tradition many call Hinduism. I also borrow from Buddhism, especially Tibetan Dzogchen, from the Stoics and from science. I'm an old white guy borrowing from traditions I wasn't born into, so I try to borrow with reverence. If I've oversimplified something or got it wrong, that's my ignorance, and I'd want to know.

I've Been Down Here Before10 / 11

Practice

I am loving awareness

We have to get out of our minds. Our thinking minds. I'll tell you how I do it…Ram Dass · "I Am Loving Awareness," with East Forest, 2019
  1. Sit comfortably. Let your shoulders drop.
  2. Put a hand on the middle of your chest. Ram Dass called this the spiritual heart.
  3. Take a few deep breaths into that spot. Breathe in love. Breathe out love.
  4. Silently say I am loving awareness. Slowly, again and again.
  5. When a thought pulls you away, notice it. Love it too. Then come back to the words.
  6. Come back to it every day. It was about a month before I felt the load lift.

Give it a month.

While that takes root, we start with the Basics. First, what the alarm is and why it won't stop ringing.

I've Been Down Here Before11 / 11

Chapter 2

The Alarm

The first of the Basics. Before any levers or any breathing, it helps to know what you're dealing with.

The Alarm1 / 10

Anxiety isn't a weakness. It's an alarm, and it's doing its job.

It's the oldest safety system you own. Every one of your ancestors had it, and every one of them lived long enough to pass it on. When it senses a threat, it floods the body with adrenaline and picks one of five settings.

  • FightPush back.
  • FlightGet out.
  • FreezeGo still and hope it passes.
  • FawnKeep the threat happy.
  • FlopShut down.

"Fawn" was named by the therapist Pete Walker. "Flop," going limp, comes from trauma research.

The Alarm2 / 10

It can't tell toast from a house fire.

When the danger is real, you want this system fast and loud. A car swerves toward you and you've jumped before you've thought. That's the alarm, and you'd be dead without it. So there's no cure for anxiety, because it isn't a disease. It's equipment. Be wary of anyone selling a cure.

But the alarm has one flaw. It can't tell a burnt breakfast from a burning house. A sharp email, a quiet room, a Sunday night, and it goes off exactly as if a bear had walked in.

What you're after is an alarm that stops going off for burnt toast.

The Alarm3 / 10

The alarm isn't the trouble. The trouble starts with the second fear.

The first fear is the alarm doing its job. Your heart speeds up. On its own, that would pass in a minute or two. But then you notice your heart and wonder if it's a heart attack. That thought is the second fear, fear of the fear. It pumps more adrenaline, which speeds your heart, which seems to prove the thought. Now you have a loop, and the loop can run for hours.

Plenty of people ride this loop all the way to the emergency room, and hear that it was "just" anxiety.

Chest pain always deserves a doctor the first time. Once your heart has been checked, you can stop arguing with it.

The Alarm4 / 10

Ride the loop enough, and the nerves learn it.

Dr. Claire Weekes called this sensitization: nerves conditioned to over-react, so ordinary stress brings unusually strong feelings, sometimes with alarming speed. The pounding heart, the churning stomach, the sweaty palms. It's the same way a muscle gets stronger from use. Run the loop enough times and the alarm gets quicker to fire and slower to stand down, until it's going off at things that never used to touch you.

Sensitization is what needs healing. The alarm itself is fine.

That's good news, even if it doesn't feel like it. Nothing is broken. Your nerves learned something, and what gets learned can be unlearned.

The Alarm5 / 10

Two things keep the alarm ringing, and both are made of thought.

So if the alarm itself is fine, what keeps it going off? Weekes named two culprits.

Bewilderment

Trying to work out what's wrong with you, over and over, and never finding the answer.

Fear

Fear of the symptoms themselves. Avoiding whatever brings them on, and dreading the next wave.

You can't think your way out of a knot made of thinking.

So the first job isn't to think harder. It's to give the body what it needs so the alarm can stand down, and to stop feeding the second fear. That's what the Basics are for.

The Alarm6 / 10

A companion

Dr. Claire Weekes

1903–1990

An Australian doctor who had been down the hole herself. At 26 she was misdiagnosed with tuberculosis, and the fear left her anxious for about two years.

She qualified in medicine at 42, became a GP, and spent the rest of her life writing to anxious people in plain language. Her first book, Self Help for Your Nerves (1962), sold several hundred thousand copies. In the US it was published as Hope and Help for Your Nerves.

Her advice was radical for its time: stop fighting it.

Fighting the feeling is the second fear in action. Every push adds adrenaline. She taught four words instead, and they're on the next page.

Hope and Help for Your NervesClaire WeekesBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Alarm7 / 10
Face.Turn toward the feeling instead of running from it.
Accept.Let it be there, however strange it feels.
Float.Don't tense up and push. Loosen, and let it carry you past, the way water holds a body that stops thrashing.
Let time pass.Your nerves settle on their own schedule, not yours.

The four words are Weekes's own. The lines beside them are a summary.

The Alarm8 / 10

You can't stop the first fear. You can decline the second.

The first fear is the body, and it's fast. It will have fired before you know it. The second is a thought, and thoughts can be interrupted. That's the job, and it's learnable. Every tool in the rest of the Basics is a way to interrupt the second fear before it gets going, or to make the body too settled to join in.

The Alarm9 / 10

Practice

5 · 4 · 3 · 2 · 1

This is a grounding exercise, and it's the one tool in this book for the moment anxiety comes as panic. You go through your five senses, one at a time, and name what each one finds. Five things you can see. Four you can touch. Three you can hear. Two you can smell. One you can taste. Out loud if you can, in your head if you can't.

Here's why it works. Panic is the second fear running in a loop: a thought about the body, more adrenaline, a worse thought. Your senses can't join that loop, because they only ever work in the present. The moment you go looking for the fourth thing you can touch, your attention has to leave the loop and come into the room. The thoughts lose their fuel. The alarm gets a chance to wind down.

It takes about two minutes. Use it the moment you feel the wave starting, not after it has crested. Use it in a meeting, in the car, in bed at 3 a.m. Nobody around you has to know.

  • 5things you can see
  • 4things you can touch
  • 3things you can hear
  • 2things you can smell
  • 1thing you can taste

It's hard to remember in the moment. Ask someone you love to record these five questions on your phone, in their voice. Finish with three slow breaths, each out-breath longer than the in-breath. The next two chapters explain why that helps.

This practice sits in the corner of every page of this book, under the button marked 5·4·3·2·1. Tap it any time.

Now you know what the alarm is and how the loop keeps it ringing. Next come the levers: the plain, physical things that decide how hot the alarm runs before a single thought arrives.

The Alarm10 / 10

Chapter 3

The Levers

These are the Basics: water, food, sleep, caffeine, alcohol, what you feed your mind, and moving your body. Nothing here is clever, and that's the point. A sensitized alarm can't settle in a body that's dry, hungry, tired and wired. Each of these is a lever that can turn a bad loop around, and most of them cost nothing.

The Levers1 / 11

Drink the water. Eat the meal. Start there.

Why begin with something so ordinary? Because the alarm reads the body before it reads the world. A body that's running low feels, from the inside, a lot like a body in danger. Thirst and hunger are small alarms of their own, and the big alarm hears them.

Water keeps your blood moving, helps you digest, eases your joints and helps you take in what you eat. It's the easiest lever on the board.

Eat as best you can. If anxiety kills your appetite, you may have to make yourself eat at first. If eating isn't the problem, eating a little better helps you stay level. Long gaps without food and big swings in blood sugar feel shaky and jittery, and shaky and jittery is exactly what the second fear is listening for.

In a 2018 survey of 3,327 adults in Iran, people who drank fewer than two glasses of water a day were more likely to be depressed than people who drank five or more. Anxiety leaned the same way, but that link didn't hold once other factors were accounted for. A one-time survey can't show which causes which.

The Levers2 / 11

A tired brain braces for the worst.

Aim for seven hours or more. That's the floor sleep scientists set for adults. Short of it, the brain's alarm centres run hot and the part that talks them down runs cold. You wake already braced, and the day hasn't started.

In 2013, researchers at Berkeley kept 18 healthy young adults awake all night, then scanned their brains while they waited to see unpleasant pictures. Without sleep, the amygdala and the anterior insula, two parts of the brain's alarm, fired harder while they waited. The more anxious someone was by nature, the bigger the jump in the insula.

Sleep is the lever the others lean on.

Goldstein and colleagues, Journal of Neuroscience, 2013. Seven hours or more is the 2015 consensus of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society.

The Levers3 / 11

Caffeine does a good impression of anxiety.

Restless, jittery, heart racing, sweaty, headachy, can't sleep. Caffeine and anxiety share a list. Caffeine works by sitting in the docks meant for adenosine, the chemical that tells your brain to slow down. The message never lands.

400 mg a day: the FDA's line for most healthy adults 2 to 3 twelve-ounce cups of coffee

How sensitive people are varies a lot. If you panic easily, your line may sit well below that. And because caffeine feels like anxiety, it feeds the second fear directly: your heart races from the coffee, your mind reads the racing heart as danger, and the loop is off. Cut back slowly, over a week or two, or the headaches will convince you it was a bad idea.

Caffeine can even cause an anxiety disorder of its own. The DSM-5 lists caffeine-induced anxiety disorder as a type of substance-induced anxiety disorder.

The Levers4 / 11

Alcohol borrows calm from tomorrow.

Alcohol boosts GABA, the brain's main brake, so the first drink feels like relief. Drink often and the brain adapts by easing off its own brakes. When the alcohol wears off, the alarm runs hotter than where you started.

If you drink every day, talk to a doctor before you stop. Withdrawal from heavy drinking can bring seizures, and it can be life-threatening.

The curve is a sketch of the pattern, not a measurement.

The Levers5 / 11

The levers are wired together. That's how they ganged up on me.

Obvious, right? Here's how it went. I couldn't sleep. My brain ran all night on everything it was worried about. I'd wake up tired and get through the day on espresso. The shots took the place of water, and the caffeine kept me up. So the next night was worse, and the next day took more shots.

Tired, dry, wired and weaker, round and round until I crashed. That's sensitization being built, one loop at a time.

To break it, I pulled four levers at once.

  • No more espresso
  • Less caffeine
  • More water
  • More sleep

Pull one lever and the others start to move.

The Levers6 / 11

Your feed is a lever too.

The levers so far all live in the body. But what you pour into your mind is a lever too. Is what you scroll feeding the alarm or settling it? Outrage, doom and other people's highlight reels are burnt toast, served all day, and the alarm goes off for every slice. You choose more of your feed than it feels like. Mute what winds you up. Follow what steadies you. Fill the quiet with music and voices that leave you calmer.

Quieting the mind could be another name for this whole book. The breath gets the next chapter. Stillness comes later.

A 2010 review of 39 studies and 1,140 people called mindfulness-based therapy "a promising intervention for treating anxiety and mood problems in clinical populations." Chapter 6 shows how what you feed the mind wears its grooves.

The Levers7 / 11

Move. Harder, when you can.

The alarm readies the body to run or fight. Movement is what it was readying you for. Give it the run, and the adrenaline gets used up instead of sitting in your chest looking for a reason.

Exercise is a real treatment for anxiety. A 2018 review pooled 15 trials and 675 patients with clinical anxiety. Exercise programmes eased anxiety compared with waiting, and the harder programmes did more than the gentle ones.

Start where your body is. A walk counts.

Aylett, Small and Bower, BMC Health Services Research, 2018. If you have a heart condition, or haven't exercised in a long time, check with your doctor first.

The Levers8 / 11

Do the work. Miss the shot.

Pick up the work in front of you, however anxious you are, and do it. Small, steady action snowballs. Leaning into what scares you, a step at a time, is the heart of cognitive behavioural therapy, one of the best-tested treatments for anxiety. In yoga it's karma yoga, the yoga of action, the second of the three paths from chapter 1. Chapter 13 gives it a whole chapter. For now, it's a lever: avoiding the thing teaches the alarm it was right, and doing the thing teaches it to stand down.

You'll fall. Everyone does. The ones who get somewhere get up and dust themselves off. Act and learn. Don't debate and wait.

Michael Jordan said it best.

I've missed more than 9,000 shots in my career. I've lost almost 300 games. 26 times I've been trusted to take the game-winning shot and missed. I've failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed.Michael Jordan · Nike's "Failure" ad, 1997

There's a Latin phrase for doing the work however hard it gets: amor fati, love your fate. Nietzsche made it famous. Chapter 13 comes back to it.

The Levers9 / 11

Be kind to yourself. You're eight. You're eighty.

Kindness is the last lever, and it's the one that decides whether you keep pulling the others. Start where you are. This isn't a race, and it isn't a list to judge yourself by. Comparison is the thief of joy.

We save our harshest judgments for ourselves. When I catch myself at it, I picture the judgment landing on my 8-year-old self, learning to write and getting frustrated. Or on my 80-year-old self, who can't work out the technology of the day. That's me in another season. If you think you're above that, you aren't.

Give yourself that compassion first. Then give it to everyone. They're eight and eighty too.

Dr. Becky Kennedy, a clinical psychologist, the founder of Good Inside and the author of a 2022 book by the same name, gives parents a tool for this. She calls it the most generous interpretation, or MGI. When someone's behaviour sets you off, ask: what's the most generous explanation for it? Her example is a boy who hits his sister. One reading is that he's cold-hearted. The most generous one is that sharing is hard. She's careful to add that a generous reading doesn't make the behaviour okay. It just lets you deal with the person instead of the verdict.

Here's what I've noticed, in kids and in grown-ups and in myself. When someone is struggling, the most generous interpretation is usually the true one, and it's usually this: the basics haven't been met. They're tired. They're hungry. They're overwhelmed, or they've been running on coffee and no water since morning. That's the whole of this chapter, read backward. Before you decide what's wrong with you, or with them, check the levers.

So the kindest question, when the alarm is loud, is rarely "what's wrong with me?" It's "when did I last eat, sleep, drink, or move?"

Jordan Peterson writes in 12 Rules for Life (2018) that people are better at giving their pets their medicine than taking their own. I couldn't find a study that measured it, and plenty of pet owners miss doses too. You may recognize the feeling anyway.

12 Rules for LifeJordan B. PetersonBook ↗Audiobook ↗
Good InsideBecky KennedyBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Levers10 / 11

Practice

Pull one lever

Here are the Basics as a board of levers. The green band on each one is the safe zone. When the levers sit in their zones, this is roughly how a person feels. Tap Neglect them to see what happens when they're left alone for a few weeks, and then pick the one you'll pull back first.

Levers in their zones. Rested, watered, fed, moving. The alarm has nothing to feed on.

  1. Look at the board as it is for you right now. Which lever is furthest out of its zone?
  2. Pick one. Skip the hardest. Take the one you'll actually pull.
  3. Shrink it to the smallest step that moves it. A glass of water before the first coffee. Lights out twenty minutes earlier. Mute one account. A ten-minute walk.
  4. Do it every day this week.
  5. Watch what else moves.

The Levers11 / 11

Chapter 4

The Long Exhale

The last of the Basics, and the one I'd keep if I could only keep one. Before anything else, breathe in and sigh it out. Then once more, louder.

The Long Exhale1 / 11

Of all the body's automatic systems, only one comes with a handle.

Left alone. The others run how they like.

The levers in the last chapter work over days and weeks. The alarm works in seconds. You need something that works in seconds too.

Your heart, your gut, your sweat and your pupils all run themselves. You can't tell any of them to calm down. Try it. Order your heart to slow. Nothing happens.

Your breath runs itself too, all night long. But you can take it over whenever you like. Leave the handle alone and the other four run however they like, faster and hotter, feeding the alarm. Turn it slowly, and they fall into step, because they're all wired to the same nerve, and the breath is the one place you can reach it.

That makes the breath the most powerful tool you have.

Yoga calls breath work pranayama, the fourth of the eight limbs in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

The Yoga Sutras of PatanjaliSri Swami SatchidanandaBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Long Exhale2 / 11

Soft food, small jaws, crowded noses.

But most of us hold the handle wrong, and the reason goes back thousands of years. James Nestor tells the story in Breath. Cooking meant less chewing. Farming softened food further. Then, in the last 300 years, soft processed food nearly stopped us chewing at all.

Chewing is what builds a roomy jaw. Without it, mouths grow too small for their teeth, the roof of the mouth pushes up into the nose, and the airway narrows. When the nose gets crowded, we breathe through the mouth.

A primate our size would spend almost half its waking day eating. We spend about a twentieth. Old skulls back Nestor on the jaw. Farmers' lower jaws grew a different shape from hunter-gatherers', and teeth stopped fitting so well.

Breath: The New Science of a Lost ArtJames NestorBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Long Exhale3 / 11

Breathe in through your nose.

Air that comes in through the nose takes the long way, past three curled shelves called turbinates. By the time it reaches your lungs it has been

slowed,filtered,warmedand moistened.

The mouth skips all of it. Mouth breathing tends to be fast, shallow and high in the chest, which is exactly how you breathe when the alarm is on. Do it all day and you're telling the body, quietly, that something is wrong. Breathe through your nose most of the time, and always on the in-breath.

A nose that's blocked most of the time is worth a visit to the doctor.

The Long Exhale4 / 11

The in-breath is the gas. The out-breath is the brake.

The nose is for the in-breath. The out-breath has a job of its own. The vagus nerve runs from your brainstem down to your heart, lungs and gut. Its name is Latin for wandering. It's the main line of the rest-and-digest system, the opposite of the alarm. When it's active, the heart slows, digestion starts up again and the body gets the message that the danger has passed.

On every in-breath it eases off the heart, and your pulse quickens a little. On every out-breath it presses again, and your pulse slows. Make the out-breath longer and more of every minute is spent on the brake. That's the main trick of this chapter. Most of the patterns that follow are different ways of doing it, and the one that isn't, the box breath, has a job of its own.

This rise and fall is called respiratory sinus arrhythmia. It's normal, a sign of a healthy heart, and it grows when you breathe slowly.

The Long Exhale5 / 11

Prayer found the rhythm first.

In 2001, researchers in Italy had 23 people recite the Ave Maria in Latin, and then a yoga mantra. Both slowed breathing to about six breaths a minute. Heart rate, blood pressure and breath began to rise and fall together.

The authors wondered if the rosary, and mantras, caught on partly because they slow the breath to this rhythm. James Nestor puts the sweet spot at five and a half breaths a minute.

The most efficient breathing rhythm occurred when the length of respirations and total breaths per minute were locked into a spooky symmetry: 5.5-second inhales followed by 5.5-second exhales, which works out almost exactly to 5.5 breaths a minute.James Nestor · Breath, 2020

I tip it toward the exhale, for the reason on the last page: a longer out-breath is more time on the brake. This is the everyday pace, the one for sitting at your desk or lying in bed, and it's the one the practice at the end of this chapter uses.

5 in · 6 out seconds, through the nose ≈ 5.5 breaths a minute, with the brake on a little longer

Bernardi and colleagues, BMJ, 2001. Chapter 10 has a breathing cell set to this pace.

The Long Exhale6 / 11

Don't grade yourself.

  • Forget the stopwatch.Lengthen both breaths from wherever you start, then make the out-breath the longer one. That's all the counting you need.
  • Wandering is normal.However many times you drift, come back. Think "rising" on the in-breath and "falling" on the out-breath, or feel your belly move, or the cool air at the tip of your nose.
  • Ocean breath.Narrow the back of your throat a little, as if fogging a mirror with your mouth closed. The breath makes a soft sea sound and stretches out. In yoga this is ujjayi.
  • Lost? Find the exhale.When nothing else works, make the out-breath long.
The Long Exhale7 / 11

A pacer

Box breath: four even sides

Picture a square. Breathe in up one side for a count of four. Hold across the top for four. Breathe out down the far side for four. Hold along the bottom for four. Then start again. In yoga it's sama vritti, the even breath, with a pause after the in-breath and another after the out-breath. Follow the dot.

Breathe in · 4Hold · 4Breathe out · 4Hold · 4

Ten rounds, about two and a half minutes, then let the breath go back to normal.

Here the in-breath and out-breath stay even, so this one doesn't push you toward sleep. It steadies you and sharpens you. The counting gives the mind one simple job, which crowds out the second fear, and the slow, even pace tells the body nothing is chasing it. That makes it the pattern for the middle of the day: before a hard conversation, in the car outside the meeting, when you need to be calm and still switched on. The next two tip the balance toward the exhale, and they're the ones for winding down.

Skip the holds if you're pregnant, or have high blood pressure, heart or lung problems. Breathe in for four and out for four instead.

The Long Exhale8 / 11

A pacer

4 · 7 · 8, the one for winding down

Dr. Andrew Weil's take on an old pranayama. Where the box breath is even, this one is weighted all the way toward the exhale, so it's the pattern for the end of the day, for lying in bed with a racing mind, or for coming down after a wave has passed. Rest the tip of your tongue on the ridge just behind your upper front teeth, and keep it there.

In through the nose · 4Hold · 7Out through the mouth · 8

Breathe in quietly through the nose for four. Hold for seven. Breathe out through the mouth with a whoosh for eight, twice as long as the in-breath. The long hold lets the lungs fill, and the long whoosh is the brake held down hard.

Start with four rounds, twice a day. After a month you can work up to eight. If the hold is hard, count faster. The ratio matters more than the seconds. It can make you light-headed at first, so do it sitting or lying down.

The same caution: no holds if you're pregnant, or have high blood pressure, heart or lung problems.

The Long Exhale9 / 11

A pacer you can hear

Become a Wizard of Ah: the exhale you can hear

Om is three sounds, A, U and M. In Tibet's Dzogchen tradition the first one stands alone, a white letter A, said "ah," pictured inside a sphere of rainbow light. One short Buddhist sutra fits the whole Perfection of Wisdom into this single letter.

Breathe out completely. Breathe in all the way to your toes, and let it go. Three times, louder each time.

Ahhhh.

Ahhhhhhh!

Ahhhhhhhhhh!

To say ah you have to open your mouth and let the jaw and tongue go loose. It's a long exhale you can hear, and it's hard to do without smiling.

Lorin Roche, in The Radiance Sutras: "That gasp of 'Ah!' or 'Aha!' is a natural mantra." In a 2023 Stanford study, a month of five-minute sighing sessions, with long exhales, lifted people's mood more than the same time spent in mindfulness meditation.

The Radiance SutrasLorin RocheBook ↗
The Long Exhale10 / 11

Practice

Twenty minutes of long exhales

  1. Sit, or lie on your back. Drop your shoulders, loosen your belly, and let your tongue fall from the roof of your mouth.
  2. Breathe all the way out. Then let a few ordinary breaths come and go.
  3. Lengthen both breaths, in through the nose. Then let the out-breath run longer than the in-breath. In for 5, out for 6, if counting helps.
  4. When your mind wanders, come back. Rising, falling.
  5. Twenty minutes, once a day. Twice if you can.

If this is the only thing you learn here, it's worth the price of admission.

That's the Basics. You know what the alarm is and how the second fear keeps it ringing. You have the levers, and you have the breath. Everything from here on is about the mind, and you'll do all of it better with a settled body. When a later chapter is hard going, that's your cue to come back here, not to push harder.

Time, habit, the knots, and the character you've been playing.

Chapter 5

It Is Always Now

The Basics settle the body. Now we turn to the mind, and start loosening your grip on what you think you know, beginning with time.

It Is Always Now1 / 11

There has only ever been now.

It is always now. This might sound trite, but it is the truth.Sam Harris · Waking Up, 2014

Every memory you have was made in a now. Every plan you carry out will happen in one. I call the habit of noticing this nowness awareness. It's the meditative state, carried into an ordinary day.

Why does this matter for anxiety? Because the alarm from chapter 2 only has one job: deal with what's in front of you. Almost all anxious thought is about somewhere else, a past you're replaying or a future you're rehearsing. The alarm can't tell the difference, so it fires for both. Bring attention back to now and you've taken away most of what it was firing at.

Right now, is anything in the room asking you to fight, run or freeze? Almost always, nothing is.

Waking UpSam HarrisBook ↗Audiobook ↗
It Is Always Now2 / 11

Past and future have no floor to stand on.

Going over the past would make sense if you owned a time machine. You don't. So you spend the one thing you do have, this moment, on something you can't change.

Rehearsing false futures feels like planning. Mostly it piles a second worry on top of the first and takes you further from where you want to be.

You can visit. You can't live there.

It Is Always Now3 / 11

Most of what you fear hasn't happened.

There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.Seneca · Letter 13 · trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917

Seneca, a Roman Stoic, wrote that to a worried friend nearly two thousand years ago. His advice was “not to be unhappy before the crisis comes.” It may never come. It certainly hasn't come yet.

Letters from a StoicSenecaBook ↗Audiobook ↗
It Is Always Now4 / 11

The argument you won at 3 a.m. and never had.

Have you ever been so angry with someone that you lay awake half the night rehearsing everything you'd say? Over and over?

Then the moment came, and it went nothing like that. Most of it never got said. All the rehearsal bought you was a short night, and you showed up tired, groggy and in a worse mood.

That's suffering in imagination. The words you never said kept the anger alive all night.

And notice what else it cost you. The lost sleep is one of the Basics, so the next day's alarm ran hotter, and the loop got one turn tighter. The mind and the body feed each other in both directions.

Worry is exhausting. Thinking itself burns very little: your brain uses about a fifth of your energy at rest, and hard thinking adds only a sliver. The lost sleep and an alarm humming all night are what wear you out. (The story that chess grandmasters burn 6,000 calories a day doesn't hold up.)

It Is Always Now5 / 11

How many nows in a day?

24 × 60 × 60 hours, minutes, seconds = 86,400 moments of now, every day

Each one comes once. Spend it stewing over a past you can't change, or a false future that probably won't happen, and it's gone.

Spend it here, and it's yours.

It Is Always Now6 / 11

So what do you do with a thought? Don't serve it tea.

Let thoughts come and go. Just don't serve them tea.Shunryu Suzuki, as his student remembered it

You can't stop thoughts from arriving, and you don't need to. Leave the front door and the back door open. A thought walks in. You notice it. It walks out the back.

Serving it tea means sitting it down, answering it, and topping up its cup until it stays the night. The second fear from chapter 2 is tea service. The thought "is this a heart attack?" walks in, and instead of letting it pass you argue with it, check your pulse, and pour another cup.

Shunryu Suzuki was a Zen teacher. His student David Chadwick remembered this line, which starts with leaving the front and back doors open, and put it in his biography of Suzuki, Crooked Cucumber (1999). Chadwick couldn't find it in the transcripts of Suzuki's talks.

Crooked CucumberDavid ChadwickBook ↗Audiobook ↗
It Is Always Now7 / 11

Kathmandu, 1967

Just be here now.

Richard Alpert was 35, a former Harvard psychology professor, a long way from home and looking for answers. In Kathmandu he met a very tall young American from Laguna Beach, California, who went by Bhagavan Das. Alpert felt sure this young man knew what he wanted to know, and followed him across India.

I would say to him, “Did I ever tell you the time I was in Mexico flying?” And he’d say, “Don’t think about the past, just be here now.” “How long do you suppose we are going to be on this trip?” “Don’t think about the future, just be here now.” I’d say, “Boy, do I feel crummy.” He’d say, “Emotions are like waves, watch them disappear into the distance.”Ram Dass · Here We All Are, 1969

Bhagavan Das took him to his own teacher, Neem Karoli Baba, who named him Ram Dass. Ram Dass told this story in his 1969 talks, Here We All Are, and two years later published Be Here Now.

It Is Always Now8 / 11

The promise

Then Bhagavan Das made Alpert a promise.

If you can be here now, when then is now, you will have super-consciousness and super-energy and you will know just what to do.Ram Dass · Here We All Are, 1969

I can tell you it's true. When life really challenged me, being here gave me more clarity and more energy than I knew I had. And I knew just what to do.

I'll tell you how I found out in chapter 14.

It Is Always Now9 / 11

Holding on is what's wearing you out.

To hold your breath is to lose your breath.Alan Watts · The Wisdom of Insecurity, 1951

The book's subtitle is A Message for an Age of Anxiety. The anxious mind holds on. To the past, to the plan, to the feeling of being in control. All that holding costs energy.

Let go, and the energy comes back to you, free. This whole book came out of that free energy.

The Wisdom of InsecurityAlan WattsBook ↗Audiobook ↗
It Is Always Now10 / 11

Practice

Doors open, no tea

The breath is your shortcut back. It runs on its own, but the moment you pay attention to it, your mind has to come with you, because breathing only ever happens now.

  1. Sit somewhere quiet. Set a timer for five minutes.
  2. Take three slow breaths through your nose, each out-breath longer than the in-breath. Then let the breath run on its own, and just feel it.
  3. You're the house. The front door and the back door are both open.
  4. When a thought walks in, give it one word: past or future.
  5. Then let it walk out the back. Don't answer it. Don't pour the tea. Go back to the breath.
  6. When the timer goes, notice how few of your visitors were about now.

Let them come. Let them go. You stay here.

You'll notice the same few visitors keep coming back. That's not an accident. The next chapter is about why thoughts wear ruts, and how to carve better ones.

Next in the scroll06 · Grooves
It Is Always Now11 / 11

Chapter 6

Grooves

Water carves the groove. Then the groove steers the water. That's why the same worries keep finding you.

Grooves1 / 11

Every thought you think leaves a mark, and the mark pulls the next one in.

SaṃskāraAn impression. The mark a thought, a feeling or an action leaves behind, like a footprint in sand.
VāsanāThe pull those marks create. A tendency waiting for its moment, like a marble that keeps rolling into the same dip.

Yoga could fill a whole course with these two words. For this book, think of them as the grooves your habits run in. Each time you repeat a thought, a feeling or an action, its groove gets a little deeper, and the deeper it gets, the more easily the next thought falls into it.

That's sensitization from chapter 2, described from the inside. The alarm didn't just fire. It fired the same way, about the same things, so often that the firing became a groove. The good news is in the second half of this chapter: grooves can be carved on purpose.

Grooves2 / 11

Hot water on jelly: how a channel digs itself

If you take a jelly, solidified and turned out onto a plate, and you trickle very hot water onto the top, it will run off onto the plate and leave behind a faint channel where the hot water melted the jelly. If you now pour more hot water, it will tend to run into the same channels as before, since these offer the line of least resistance, and deepen the channels.Edward de Bono · The Mechanism of Mind, 1969

Keep pouring, and soon the water can't go anywhere else.

Thoughts run in channels like that. So do moods.

De Bono was describing how memory and habit form. The link to saṃskāra and vāsanā is mine.

The Mechanism of MindEdward de BonoBook ↗
Grooves3 / 11

A story

Two wolves

A grandfather tells his grandson that a fight is going on inside him, between two wolves.

One is anger, envy, regret, self-pity, resentment and false pride.

The other is joy, peace, love, hope, kindness and generosity.

"The same fight is going on inside you," he says.

The boy thinks about it. "Which wolf will win?"

"The one you feed."

It's usually told as a Cherokee legend, but its origin is unknown. The oldest versions on record are American stories from the 1960s about two dogs, and Billy Graham told one in a 1978 book. The wolves came later. Where it came from matters less to me than what it says.

Grooves4 / 11

What I fed mine, and what I feed it now

Your feed was one of the levers in chapter 3. Here's that lever, seen as a groove. When I got low, angry or scared, I'd put on music that matched. My brain took the hint. It decided I wanted to feel that way and helped out, piling on thoughts that agreed with the worst.

So I built playlists that went the other way, and kept breath work and meditations ready for when a mood started to spiral. Moods I used to stew in for days, I can now let go of in minutes. Hours at most.

This isn't faking it. You still feel the anger, and you still deal with the real problem. Forced cheer is toxic positivity. Using spiritual talk to dodge real problems is spiritual bypassing.

Feeding the good wolf just means choosing what plays next.

Grooves5 / 11

Cells that fire together wire together.

The jelly isn't only a metaphor. Neuroscience calls this neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to rewire itself through experience. The grooves are real connections between real cells, and they get thicker with use.

In 1949 the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that when one brain cell keeps helping to fire another, the connection between them grows stronger. The neuroscientist Carla Shatz later put it in six words.

It's easier when you're young. It keeps happening your whole life. The way you think right now isn't permanent.

Hebb, The Organization of Behavior (1949). Shatz's phrase is from Scientific American, 1992.

The Organization of BehaviorD. O. HebbBook ↗
Grooves6 / 11

About 6,000 thoughts a day, and you don't have to answer any of them

≈ 6.5 shifts to a new thought, every minute 6,000+ in a waking day

In 2020, Julie Tseng and Jordan Poppenk at Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario, studied brain scans of 184 people lying still or watching films. They couldn't tell what anyone was thinking. They could see when the brain's overall pattern jumped to a new state, the way it did when a new scene began in a film. Those jumps came about six and a half times a minute. Over sixteen waking hours, that's more than 6,000.

You may have heard 60,000 a day, mostly negative and repeated. No one has found a study behind that number. In this one, people higher in neuroticism, the trait most tied to anxiety, jumped a little more often at rest.

Thousands of thoughts come and go. You're the one who hears them.

Grooves7 / 11

Whatever you do, don't think of a big yellow school bus.

Too late. People have been telling you "don't" your whole life. Don't do that, don't say this. Your brain filed each one as a rule, and a lot of what you worry about is like that bus. Someone else put it there.

Pushing a thought away doesn't work either. In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner asked people to think out loud for five minutes without thinking of a white bear, and to ring a bell whenever it came up. They rang it about once a minute.

If a friend talked to you the way your mind sometimes does, you'd stop being friends. You don't have to keep listening to that voice either.

You can't delete the bus. You can let it drive past.

So the way to change a groove isn't to fight the old one. Fighting it is more water down the same channel. You pour somewhere new, a little every day, until the new channel is the easier one. The next page gives you ten places to pour.

Wegner borrowed the white bear from Dostoevsky, who set readers the same challenge in 1863.

Grooves8 / 11

Yamas & niyamas

Ten grooves worth carving

If the mind is going to cut grooves anyway, pick good ones. The first two limbs of yoga give you ten, and they come before any work on thought. That order is on purpose, and it's the same order as this book: how you live comes before how you meditate, the way the Basics came before the mind.

YamasHow you meet the world

AhiṃsāNon-harmingThat includes the voice in your head. Trade self-criticism for kindness.
SatyaTruthfulnessDrop the masks. You're worthy without the packaging.
AsteyaNon-stealingAnxiety steals the present. Stop handing it over.
BrahmacaryaRight use of energyStop spending it on what you can't control.
AparigrahaNon-graspingHolding on is the anxious mind's habit. Letting go is the way out.

NiyamasHow you meet yourself

ŚaucaPurityClean up the habits. Make room for awe: a sunrise, the northern lights.
SantoṣaContentmentEnough, right now. Gratitude is the way in.
TapasHeat, steady effortOne thing at a time, with full focus, day after day.
SvādhyāyaSelf-studySit with yourself. Watch the mind chatter.
Īśvara praṇidhānaSurrenderLet go of the beliefs that feed the fear. This one is the whole thing.

If you aren't harming anyone, you tell the truth, you don't steal, you don't waste your energy and you don't cling, look how much less there is to be anxious about.

The Yama and Niyama, as we see, are moral trainings; without these as the basis no practice of Yoga will succeed.Swami Vivekananda · Raja Yoga, 1896

Yoga Sutras 2.30 and 2.32. Brahmacarya traditionally meant celibacy; modern yoga reads it as moderation. The one-line glosses are mine, with a debt to Deborah Adele's The Yamas & Niyamas (2009). Adele on asteya: it "calls us to live with integrity and reciprocity." On aparigraha: "Nonattachment does not mean we do not care or that we shut ourselves off from the pleasures and joy of life… We are asked to let go of the clinging to the thing, not the enjoyment of the thing."

The Yamas & NiyamasDeborah AdeleBook ↗Audiobook ↗
Raja YogaSwami VivekanandaBook ↗Audiobook ↗
Grooves9 / 11

One word answers every objection: anyway.

Before I had yoga, I had these. A mentor taught them to me. There are ten, written in 1968 by Kent M. Keith when he was a 19-year-old student at Harvard. Each one names a reason to give up, then answers it. Here are four of the ten.

People are illogical, unreasonable, and self-centered.

Love them anyway.

The good you do today will be forgotten tomorrow.

Do good anyway.

Honesty and frankness make you vulnerable.

Be honest and frank anyway.

What you spend years building may be destroyed overnight.

Build anyway.

The anxious mind will raise objections all day. You don't have to win the argument.

From "The Paradoxical Commandments" © Kent M. Keith, 1968. A version titled "Anyway" hung on the wall of Shishu Bhavan, Mother Teresa's children's home in Calcutta, which is why it's often credited to her.

The Paradoxical CommandmentsKent M. Keith · all ten, and the story behind themWebsite ↗
Grooves10 / 11

Practice

Leaf on a stream

what iftoo lateI should havebuy milkthey think
  1. Sit comfortably. Close your eyes, or rest them on one spot.
  2. Picture a slow stream, with leaves drifting by on the surface.
  3. Each time a thought shows up, set it on a leaf and watch it float away. Worries, plans, pictures, the pleasant ones too.
  4. If a leaf snags, let it sit until it moves on. Don't push the water.
  5. When you notice you've been swept downstream with a thought, climb back onto the bank. That noticing is the practice.
  6. Five minutes. Then open your eyes.

A defusion exercise from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT). It's still one of the practices I come back to most.

Let it float. That's a groove too.

Some grooves run deeper than habit. Yoga says there are five that tie up every mind, and the anxious mind most of all. The next chapter names them.

Next in the scroll07 · The Five Knots
Grooves11 / 11

Chapter 7

The Five Knots

Yoga names five knots that tie the mind up. Once you can find a knot, you can start to loosen it.

The Five Knots1 / 11

Patanjali counted five knots, and the first one ties the rest.

He called them kleshas, the afflictions. An old translation calls them "the pain-bearing obstructions." They cloud the mind and keep the suffering coming, and the first one feeds the other four. If the grooves in the last chapter are the habits of one mind, the knots are the habits of every mind. Yoga has been describing them for two thousand years, and you'll recognize all five.

  • AvidyaNot seeing clearly. The root of the rest.
  • AsmitaI-am-ness. Taking what you hold up for who you are.
  • RagaClinging to what felt good.
  • DveshaPushing away what felt bad.
  • AbhiniveshaClinging to life. The fear of death. We'll come back to this one at the very end.

Yoga Sutras 2.3 and 2.4; the old translation is Swami Vivekananda's (1896). Some teachers call the kleshas the five poisons. Tibetan Buddhism has its own five poisons, a different list that includes pride and jealousy.

The Five Knots2 / 11

Avidya · not seeing

A snake in the dark.

You walk into a dark room and there's a snake coiled on the floor. Your heart pounds. You jump back. Then someone brings a lamp, and it's a rope. It was always a rope. Nothing changed but the light.

The fear was real. The snake never was.

This is the whole of jñāna yoga in one picture. You don't fight the snake. You don't talk yourself out of being scared. You bring a lamp. Most of what an anxious mind is afraid of is rope, and this chapter is about the ways we keep seeing snakes.

The rope and the snake is one of the oldest teaching images in Advaita Vedanta, the non-dual school behind jñāna yoga. Patanjali calls avidya the field the other four knots grow in (Yoga Sutras 2.4).

The Five Knots3 / 11

Four ways to misread the rope.

Lasting?The passing, taken for the lasting. Everything changes, your body and mind included. "I'll always be like this" is this mistake.
Pure?The stained, taken for the pure. The diamond sparkles and hides what it cost to dig up. The thing you're sure would fix you sparkles too.
Pleasure?The painful, taken for the pleasant. The drink that takes the edge off tonight and sharpens it tomorrow.
Me?The not-self, taken for the Self. The costume, mistaken for the one wearing it. That's the next knot.

Yoga Sutras 2.5. Buddhism lists the same four mistakes. If you drink every day, talk to a doctor before you stop. Quitting suddenly can be dangerous.

The Five Knots4 / 11

Six funhouse mirrors the anxious mind looks in.

The anxious brain takes shortcuts. It skips part of the picture and fills the gap with the worst version. That's avidya too, and it's the second fear from chapter 2 dressed up in words. Same you, bent six ways. Once you can name the mirror you're looking in, it loses most of its power.

  • Catastroph­izing"If I mess up this presentation, I'll lose my job."
  • Over­generalization"I got nervous at one party. I'm always terrible with people."
  • Mind reading"They went quiet. They think I'm boring."
  • Emotional reasoning"I feel like a failure, so I must be one."
  • Personal­ization"My friend is upset. It must be something I did."
  • Filtering"Everyone liked it except one person. That's all I can think about."

Psychologists call these cognitive distortions. Aaron Beck described them, and David Burns made the list famous in Feeling Good (1980).

Feeling GoodDavid D. BurnsBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Five Knots5 / 11

Asmita · I-am-ness

The badges you hold up as yourself.

Patanjali calls it taking the instrument of seeing for the one who sees. You get the job and become the title. Then you retire, and the title is gone. You raise a child, and if you do it well, they leave.

If someone swears at you in a language you don't know, the words can't touch you. You give words their meaning. You give the badges theirs too.

None of them is who you are. The next chapter is about setting them down.

Yoga Sutras 2.6.

The Five Knots6 / 11

Raga · attachment

Gripping a steering wheel that isn't attached to anything.

"Attachment is that which dwells on pleasure," says Patanjali. It's the pull back toward whatever felt good. Food, shopping, a drink, a screen, a bet. No moral judgement here. The next knot causes just as much trouble. Notice that two of the levers from the Basics, caffeine and alcohol, live right here.

In anxiety, raga looks like holding on to a control that doesn't exist. Attachment to calm. To how things ought to be. To the places your triggers aren't.

Yoga Sutras 2.7, in Vivekananda's translation.

The Five Knots7 / 11

Dvesha · aversion

Every place you avoid moves the fence in.

"Aversion is that which dwells on pain." It's the dentist you put off until the cavity becomes a root canal.

On Sunday afternoons I'd start thinking about the work week, and my body would start in. If I engaged those thoughts, I could spiral until I didn't go in on Monday.

Avoiding a trigger feels like a win. Each time, the fence moves in a little, and the love and belonging you want end up on the other side of it. This is why "do the work" was a lever back in chapter 3. Every time you walk toward the thing instead of away, the fence moves back out.

Yoga Sutras 2.8. At its hardest, avoidance becomes agoraphobia: fear of places where escape or help might be hard to reach, until even leaving home is too much. It often follows panic attacks, and it can be treated. If your world is shrinking, tell your doctor.

The Five Knots8 / 11

The middle path

Neither too tight nor too loose.

Seeing all this clinging, it's tempting to give everything up. That doesn't work either. Too much of almost anything turns harmful. Even water, drunk compulsively, can be dangerous.

Before he was the Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama tried to starve his way to freedom, and it nearly killed him. In his first sermon he named two extremes to avoid: a life spent chasing pleasure, and a life spent punishing yourself. Between them runs the middle path.

There are two extremes, O Bhikkhus, which the man who has given up the world ought not to follow—the habitual practice, on the one hand, of those things whose attraction depends upon the passions, and especially of sensuality … and the habitual practice, on the other hand, of asceticism (or self-mortification), which is painful, unworthy, and unprofitable. There is a middle path, O Bhikkhus, avoiding these two extremes, discovered by the Tathāgata—a path which opens the eyes, and bestows understanding, which leads to peace of mind, to the higher wisdom, to full enlightenment, to Nirvāna!The Buddha · Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta · tr. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1881

Hold on less. Push away less.

The sermon was first put into English by T. W. Rhys Davids in 1881, which is the translation above. The tuned string is the Buddha's image too, from his advice to the monk Sona.

The Five Knots9 / 11

Let it RAIN: a middle path for one worry at a time.

RAIN is a way to meet a worry without clinging to it or running from it, which is the middle path from the last page, made practical. The four letters are four steps. Say there's a party tonight and you're dreading it.

Recognize.Name what's here. "I'm feeling anxious about going out tonight."
Allow.Let it be there without pushing it away. "It's okay to feel this way."
Investigate.Get curious, kindly. "I'm worried people will judge me, or I'll say something embarrassing, or I'll see someone I've been avoiding."
Non-identifi­cation.See that the feeling is passing through you. It isn't you. "Going out adds some uncertainty. I'll do my best. True friends won't care if I say something embarrassing."

The meditation teacher Michele McDonald created RAIN, and Tara Brach made it widely known. Brach now teaches the N as Nurture: meeting yourself with kindness.

The Five Knots10 / 11

Practice

RAIN on one worry

  1. Sit somewhere quiet. Pick one worry that's with you today. A small one is fine.
  2. Recognize. Name it. The thought, the feeling, where it sits in your body.
  3. Allow. Let it be there. You don't have to fix it or push it out.
  4. Investigate. Get curious, with kindness. What set this off? What does this feeling want from you?
  5. Non-identification. Will this pass? Notice that you're the one noticing it.

Your page

Saved only on this device.

Let it rain. Rain passes.

Four of the five knots, named. The fifth waits for the last chapter. And the second one, taking your badges for yourself, needs more room than a page. It gets the next chapter.

Next in the scroll08 · The Spacesuit
The Five Knots11 / 11

Chapter 8

The Spacesuit

The second knot, asmita, gets its own chapter. You've worn the suit so long, you think it's you.

The Spacesuit1 / 11

Soon after you're born, the somebody training starts.

The people around you already know who they are, and they teach you who you are. They mean well, and you need some of it to get by. Ram Dass called this somebody training. He called what it builds a spacesuit: a body, with a brain to steer it, for living on this plane.

Then you walk into a room full of other spacesuits. Do I look okay? What should I say? Will they like me? What if I embarrass myself? A huge share of everyday anxiety is the suit worrying about the other suits.

Everybody is reinforcing their structure of the universe over and over again, and you meet like two huge things meeting. We enter into these conspiracies. You say, I'll make believe you are who you think you are if you make believe I am who I think I am.Ram Dass · Here We All Are, 1969
The Spacesuit2 / 11

You can take it off. Something is still there when you do.

You've been somebody long enough. You spent the first half of your life becoming somebody. Now you can work on becoming nobody, which is really somebody. For when you become nobody there is no tension, no pretense, no one trying to be anyone or anything. The natural state of the mind shines through unobstructed, and the natural state of the mind is pure love.Ram Dass · Becoming Nobody, 2019

What's left is what the Upanishads call the Self, with a capital S. It's plain awareness, steady and unchanging. Nothing needs to be added to it.

If you know, you see, that I, in the sense of the person, the front, the ego, doesn't really exist, then it won't go to your head too badly if you wake up and discover your god.Alan Watts

You're under no obligation to keep playing the character.

You'll still wear the suit to work. The difference is knowing it's a suit. Ram Dass talks about all of this in the film Becoming Nobody (2019).

The Spacesuit3 / 11

Then there's the part of the suit you keep in the dark.

Carl Jung called it the shadow: everything you hide, the weaknesses, desires, instincts and failings you'd rather not take credit for. For an anxious mind it's a deep well of fear, judgement and shame. You can't set the suit down while you're still pretending half of it isn't there.

People will do anything, no matter how absurd, in order to avoid facing their own souls. One does not become enlightened by imagining figures of light, but by making the darkness conscious.Carl Jung · Alchemical Studies

The work is to accept, and even love, the darkest parts of you.

It looks different for everyone, because your trauma isn't mine. You've done cringeworthy things, and you'll do more. That comes with the path.

Alchemical StudiesC. G. JungBook ↗
The Spacesuit4 / 11

Here's the hard part: you could have been anyone.

To fully accept your shadow, you have to accept that you could have been much worse. Give you different parents, a different brain, a different century and harder luck, and you might have done terrible things.

The ego recoils and says, not me. I'm saying yes, you, if the universe had pressed hard enough. Me too.

Only when you can say yes, Richard Nixon is us, and J. Edgar Hoover is us, and Mao is us… and the hippie is us, and the speed freak is us, and the heroin addict is us, and the psychotic is us, then we can get on with it. It is a reversal of figure and ground. It's going from the position where you are completely addicted to individual differences… to the point where… they are all the same.Ram Dass · Here We All Are, 1969

Figure and ground: the shapes you pick out, and the field they sit in. Flip them, and what stood out dissolves into the whole.

The Spacesuit5 / 11

Cut one bridge, and one person becomes two.

That sameness isn't only a nice idea. The next few pages are science, and they all point the same way: the solid, single "me" inside the suit is shakier than it feels. Start with what happens when one brain is cut in two. A thick band of about 200 million nerve fibres runs through the middle of your brain, joining the left half to the right. It's called the corpus callosum.

In the 1960s, surgeons cut it in a few people to stop severe epilepsy. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga tested them, and found each half could see, know and want things the other didn't. Some patients caught one hand buttoning a shirt while the other undid it. Usually the left hand was the rebel.

If my brain were surgically divided by callosotomy tomorrow, this would create at least two independent conscious minds, both of which would be psychologically continuous with the person who is now writing this paragraph. … The question of whether I would land in the left hemisphere or the right doesn't make sense—being based, as it is, on the illusion that there is a self bobbing on the stream of consciousness.Sam Harris · Waking Up, 2014

If one mind can come apart into two, maybe many minds, fully joined, would feel like one.

Each half of the brain steers the opposite hand. Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel Prize for this work.

Waking UpSam HarrisBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Spacesuit6 / 11

Point at the small pile, if you can.

A different piece of the suit: the part that overrides the alarm. Two plates: five candies on one, one candy on the other. Whichever plate you point at goes to someone else, and you get the other one.

Adults catch on fast. In a 1995 study by Sarah Boysen and Gary Berntson, chimpanzees mostly couldn't. They kept pointing at the big pile and watching it go. When cards with numerals replaced the candy, the same chimps picked the smaller number. Three-year-olds struggle in much the same way, and also do better with symbols.

Pointing at the small pile is your frontal cortex at work. It's the part of you that can do the hard thing.

It's also the part that declines the second fear, pulls a lever, and lengthens the exhale. And it runs on the Basics. Tired, hungry or hungover, it's the first part of you to go quiet, and the alarm gets the wheel.

It's one of the last parts of the brain to mature, and keeps developing into your twenties.

The Spacesuit7 / 11

13 September 1848

An iron rod through the brain, and he was "no longer Gage."

So what happens when that part of the brain breaks? Phineas Gage, a railway construction foreman near Cavendish, Vermont, was packing blasting powder into a hole in the rock when it went off. His iron rod shot in under his left cheekbone, passed behind his eye and flew out through the top of his head. Within minutes he was talking.

The equilibrium or balance, so to speak, between his intellectual faculties and animal propensities, seems to have been destroyed. He is fitful, irreverent, indulging at times in the grossest profanity (which was not previously his custom), manifesting but little deference for his fellows, impatient of restraint or advice when it conflicts with his desires, at times pertinaciously obstinate, yet capricious and vacillating, devising many plans of future operations, which are no sooner arranged than they are abandoned in turn for others appearing more feasible. A child in his intellectual capacity and manifestations, he has the animal passions of a strong man. Previous to his injury, although untrained in the schools, he possessed a well-balanced mind, and was looked upon by those who knew him as a shrewd, smart businessman, very energetic and persistent in executing all his plans of operation. In this regard his mind was radically changed, so decidedly that his friends and acquaintances said he was "no longer Gage."Dr John Harlow, who treated him · 1868

Who you are today depends on which parts of your brain are working right now.

Later research suggests Gage recovered more than the legend allows. He spent years driving stagecoaches in Chile.

The Spacesuit8 / 11

So who decided to move your hand?

In 1983 Benjamin Libet asked people to flex a wrist whenever they felt like it, and to note on a fast clock the moment they decided to. Electrodes on the scalp picked up the brain gearing up for the movement about a third of a second before people felt they'd decided.

Robert Sapolsky (Determined, 2023) and Sam Harris (Free Will, 2012) go further. Add up everything you never chose, from your genes and the hormones you met in the womb to this week's stress and the culture you were raised in. They argue there's no room left for free will.

I've come around to that, after many hours of thought. You don't have to today.

Here's why it belongs in a book about anxiety. If you didn't choose your genes, your childhood or last night's sleep, then the anxious wiring isn't a personal failing. It's weather you were born into. That's the most generous interpretation from chapter 3, applied to the whole of you. You can still pull the levers. You just stop blaming the person pulling them.

Scientists still argue over what Libet's build-up means. Anil Seth's "controlled hallucination" is a separate idea, about perception: what you experience is the brain's best guess, checked against the senses.

DeterminedRobert SapolskyBook ↗Audiobook ↗
Free WillSam HarrisBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Spacesuit9 / 11

Don't ask the centipede.

A centipede was happy quite,
Until a toad in fun
Said, "Pray, which leg moves after which?"
This raised her doubts to such a pitch,
She fell exhausted in the ditch
Not knowing how to run.Usually credited to Katherine Craster · 1871

Alan Watts liked to tell this one. Your breath, your heartbeat, your walk and most of your words run the same way, with nobody checking each step. Plenty of artists say their best work arrived like that, as if it came through them.

“I do not do anything,” should think the harmonised one, who knoweth the Essence of things; seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing, speaking, letting go, holding, opening and closing the eyes—convinced that it is the senses that move among the objects of sense.Bhagavad Gita 5.8–9 · tr. Annie Besant, 1895

The anxious mind works so hard to control everything. Maybe it never had the job.

No centipede has exactly a hundred legs. They always have an odd number of pairs. This one has twenty-one pairs.

The Spacesuit10 / 11

Practice

Put down one badge

  1. List the badges you hold up as who you are. Your job title. Parent. The reliable one. The anxious one. The one who's always fine.
  2. Notice which ones you defend hardest, or most dread losing. Those are holding up the most anxiety.
  3. Choose one and set it down for a day.
  4. When you catch yourself reaching for it, notice who's reaching.
  5. That night, write down what happened.

Your page

Saved only on this device.

Set it down and see who's still here.

That ends the second movement. You've watched the mind: how it lives outside of now, how it wears grooves, how it ties itself in knots, and how it mistakes the suit for the one wearing it. The third movement asks a bigger question. If you aren't the suit, where exactly do you begin?
