Chapter 9

The Sliver

Before we ask where you begin, a chapter on how little of the world you were ever shown. The whole moon is up there every night. You see the lit part and call it the moon.

The Sliver1 / 11

Your brain thinks that with enough information it could figure it all out.

That's the anxious mind's quiet bargain. With enough information it could work everything out. Then it would know, and then it could rest. It's the bewilderment from chapter 2, the endless trying to work out what's wrong, and it never pays off, because the deal was never possible.

I'm going to ask you to give that idea up. Three things stand in the way: how little of the world comes in through your senses, how little of that the brain can handle, and the shortcuts it takes to cope. This chapter takes them in that order.

Any year that passes in which you don't destroy one of your best loved ideas is a wasted year.Charlie Munger · as collected in Tao of Charlie Munger
Tao of Charlie MungerDavid ClarkBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Sliver2 / 11

This thin band is all the light you will ever see.

Radio waves, microwaves, X-rays and gamma rays are the same stuff as light. They're all electromagnetic waves, only longer or shorter. Your eyes catch the ones from about 380 to 700 nanometres long, and nothing else.

Every colour you've ever seen lives in that sliver.

Drawn to scale. Each step down the bar is ten times shorter than the one above it. The edges between bands are approximate, and the wave is only a sketch.

The Sliver3 / 11

You see in three colours.

Your eyes have three kinds of colour cone. Every colour you know is your brain mixing three signals. Other eyes are built very differently.

  • 3kinds of colour cone. You.
  • 15kinds of light receptor, at least, in the common bluebottle butterfly.
  • 12kinds of colour receptor in the mantis shrimp. Four of them catch ultraviolet.
  • 2.3×as sharp as your eyes. The wedge-tailed eagle's cones are smaller and packed tighter.

More isn't always better. With twelve channels, the mantis shrimp is worse than you at telling close colours apart. It seems to recognise colours at a glance instead of comparing them.

Each dot is one kind of receptor; hollow dots catch ultraviolet, and dot colours are only a rough guide. Vision gets more of your cortex than any other sense, roughly a fifth to a quarter of it. The often-quoted "half" is the figure for monkeys.

The Sliver4 / 11

Your hearing stops at 20,000. The moth's doesn't.

Your ears catch vibrations from about 20 to 20,000 times a second, and the top end slips as you age. Dolphins and bats call far above that. Some bats go past 200,000.

The greater wax moth hears up to about 300,000, higher than any animal we know. Bats eat moths. The moth is listening.

Drawn to scale, showing the top of each range. The moth: Moir, Jackson and Windmill, 2013.

The Sliver5 / 11

Every sense has a champion. It isn't you.

  • 175,000taste buds on a big catfish, from its whiskers to its tail. Its whole body tastes the water. You have about 2,000 to 8,000, all in your mouth.
  • 1,948smell-receptor genes in the African elephant, the record so far. Dogs have 811. You have about 400.
  • 25,000touch organs on the star-nosed mole's nose, a star about a centimetre across. It carries five times as many touch nerve fibres as your whole hand.

Every animal lives in its own sliver of the world. So do you.

The Sliver6 / 11

Even that sliver is far too much to hold.

So the senses let in a sliver. Here's the second problem: the brain can't hold even that. You have about 86 billion neurons, each wired to thousands of others. That's a lot. It still can't take in Spotify.

100,000,000 tracks on Spotify × 3 minutes each, more or less ≈ 570 years to hear them all once, without sleeping

Press play today and you'd finish around the year 2600. You can't even know Spotify the way you know your favourite song.

And you were hoping to figure out the universe.

Spotify still says "over 100 million tracks." In April 2026 its co-CEO put the real count at "something like 250 million," which would take more than 1,400 years. One rough 2010 estimate put the brain's memory at 2.5 petabytes. Nobody really knows.

The Sliver7 / 11

There's a hole in what you're seeing right now.

Close your left eye. Stare at the top cross with your right.

Slowly bring your face toward the screen, then back. Keep staring at the cross.

At one distance, the red dot disappears.

Each eye has a spot with no light receptors, where the optic nerve leaves for the brain. You never see a hole there because your brain paints over it with a guess. Try the bottom row the same way. At the right distance, the broken line looks whole.

That's the brain's habit everywhere. When something's missing, it fills in a guess and doesn't mention it.

That's the third problem. Your thinking works the same way as your eye. To keep up, the brain takes shortcuts built from past experience and fills the gaps with guesses. They usually serve you well. They're also behind a lot of everyday mistakes. The six funhouse mirrors in chapter 7 are this habit at work: a gap in what you know, filled with the worst guess, and never flagged as a guess.

The Sliver8 / 11

What is it like to be a bat?

The philosopher Thomas Nagel asked this in 1974. You could learn every fact about how a bat's sonar works and still not know what it's like, from the inside, to find a moth by its echo.

The same goes for you. Science can track which neurons fire when you see red. Nobody can yet say why any of it feels like something.

David Chalmers named this the hard problem of consciousness. It's still open.

Thomas Nagel, "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" (1974). David Chalmers, "Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness" (1995).

The Sliver9 / 11

Everything you see is your brain's best guess.

The neuroscientist Anil Seth calls perception a controlled hallucination. Your brain is always predicting what's out there. The signals from your senses keep those predictions in line, and what you experience is the prediction.

Put the three problems together. A sliver comes in, the brain keeps a fraction of the sliver, and then it fills the gaps with guesses and shows you the result as if it were the world. The anxious mind's bargain, that it could figure it all out, was never on the table. That isn't bad news. It's permission to stop trying.

We're all hallucinating all the time, including right now. It's just that when we agree about our hallucinations, we call that reality.Anil Seth · Your Brain Hallucinates Your Conscious Reality, TED 2017

It's a very good guess. You can hold it a little more lightly.

The Sliver10 / 11

Practice

Listen past the edges

  1. Sit and close your eyes. Give this one minute.
  2. Find the nearest sound. Your breath, your clothes, the hum of the room.
  3. Find the farthest sound. Traffic, wind, a bird, a neighbour's door.
  4. Find the quietest sound you can.
  5. Now listen for the edge of your hearing, where sound stops. Notice that you can't hear it.
  6. Stay there until the minute is up. Everything past the edge is still going on.

The world doesn't end where your senses do.

And if the edge of what you sense isn't the edge of the world, maybe the edge of your skin isn't the edge of you. The next chapter follows one heartbeat to find out.

Practise with Alan Watts“Listen” · Alan Watts & Boreta↗ Next in the scroll10 · Where Do You Begin?
The Sliver11 / 11

Chapter 10

Where do you begin?

The last chapter showed how little gets in. This one asks where the line around "you" really falls. Keep a hand near your chest.

Where do you begin?1 / 10

Put a hand on your chest.

Feel that?

About seventy times a minute, something in you is keeping time.

Let's follow one beat inward.

Where do you begin?2 / 10

Inside the beat

≈ 1,000,000,000 iron atoms in every red cell × 25 trillion red cells in you
Where do you begin?3 / 10

That iron wasn't made on Earth. Nothing on Earth can make it.

The iron in your blood is what carries the oxygen from each breath to every cell. Without it the breath would be useless. And iron is forged only in the last days of giant stars, and in white dwarfs that blow themselves apart. Each kind of explosion made about half the iron in the universe. Earth didn't make its iron. Earth inherited it.

Your pulse keeps time for stars that no longer exist.

Where do you begin?4 / 10

Now the breath. Where did the oxygen come from?

That's the iron. Now follow the other half of the heartbeat, the oxygen it carries. Three billion years ago the air held almost no oxygen. Less than a thousandth of one percent of what you're breathing now.

In the shallows, something tiny learned to eat sunlight. It breathed out oxygen.

Cyanobacteria. Their layered mounds, stromatolites, still grow in a few warm bays, like Shark Bay in Western Australia.

Where do you begin?5 / 10

Then the whole sea rusted.

Most of that first oxygen never reached the sky. It met the iron dissolved in the sea, and the iron rusted. Red flakes drifted down and settled, layer on layer, for hundreds of millions of years.

You can still put your hand on those layers. Much of the iron we mine today comes out of them.

Banded iron · about 2.5 billion years old
Where do you begin?6 / 10
Iron from the stars. Breath from the first sea. They met once, as stone.

They meet again in you, every few seconds. Breathe with this cell for a minute.

Breathe in · 5Breathe out · 6

In through the nose for five, out for six. The longer exhale is the part that calms the alarm (chapter 4).

Where do you begin?7 / 10

So where do you begin?

At your skin?

At your first breath?

At the first breath of the first bacteria?

At a star that blew apart before the sun was born?

The line around "me" is drawn by thought. Go looking for it in the blood, the breath, the rock and the stars, and it isn't there. This is the second knot again, asmita, at its deepest. The suit was never sealed. Air, water, iron and light pass through it every second, and always have.

For an anxious mind, this is the quietest kind of relief. A self that was never separate was never alone, and never had to hold the whole thing up.

Maybe the purpose of your life is longer than your consciousness lasts.Tom Chi · Everything Is Connected, TEDxTaipei 2015
Where do you begin?8 / 10

Now turn around and notice where you're looking from.

You can see your hands. Your knees. This page.

Can you see a head?

Where your head should be, there's only this: the whole scene, wide open.

What you are looking for is what is looking.Often credited to St. Francis of Assisi; it isn't in his writings

After Ernst Mach's self-portrait from inside his left eye (1886) and Douglas Harding's On Having No Head (1961).

On Having No HeadDouglas HardingBook ↗
Where do you begin?9 / 10

Practice

One breath, two stories

  1. Sit. Put a hand on your chest.
  2. Breathe in through the nose for five. Think sea: the first breath, handed to you.
  3. Breathe out for six. Think star: the iron that caught it.
  4. Ten rounds.
  5. Drop the words and keep breathing. Look for the line where the air stops being sky and starts being you.

The world is in you.

You've looked outward as far as the stars and found no edge. The next chapter turns the same attention inward, through the four doors yoga says lead to the one who's looking.

Next in the scroll11 · Four Doors Inward
Where do you begin?10 / 10

Chapter 11

Four Doors Inward

You've settled the body with the Basics and watched the mind. You've looked outward to the stars for the edge of you and found none. Now you go in.

Four Doors Inward1 / 11

The mind is a drunk monkey, stung by a scorpion.

How hard it is to control the mind! Well has it been compared to the maddened monkey. There was a monkey, restless by his own nature, as all monkeys are. As if that were not enough someone made him drink freely of wine, so that he became still more restless. Then a scorpion stung him. When a man is stung by a scorpion, he jumps about for a whole day; so the poor monkey found his condition worse than ever. To complete his misery a demon entered into him. What language can describe the uncontrollable restlessness of that monkey? The human mind is like that monkey, incessantly active by its own nature; then it becomes drunk with the wine of desire, thus increasing its turbulence. After desire takes possession comes the sting of the scorpion of jealousy at the success of others, and last of all the demon of pride enters the mind, making it think itself of all importance. How hard to control such a mind!Swami Vivekananda · Raja Yoga, 1896

This is what you're up against.

Everything so far has been about calming the monkey down: feeding it properly, slowing its breath, noticing its grooves and knots. Meditation is different. To make the mind your tool again, you need something to aim at besides its chatter, and a way to get underneath it.

Under the chop, the water is still.

The monkey lives up on the surface. When you're lost up there, like I was, the place meditation can take you is almost unimaginable. Eckhart Tolle says you "have a treasure within that not only includes all those things but is infinitely greater than anything the world can offer."

You reach the ocean of pure consciousness and you transcend.David Lynch, on Transcendental Meditation

Tolle's words are from The Power of Now. The filmmaker David Lynch (1946–2025) learned Transcendental Meditation in 1973 and said he never missed a sitting, twice a day, from then on. His book Catching the Big Fish (2006) says ideas are like fish, and the big ones swim deep.

Four Doors Inward3 / 11

Patanjali's last four limbs

The first two doors, you open yourself.

The Yoga Sutras list eight limbs of yoga. This is raja yoga, the path of meditation that Vivekananda taught alongside the Gita's three (chapter 1). You've met the outer limbs in this book already: the yamas and niyamas in chapter 6, how you sit, and the breath work of chapter 4. The last four turn inward, each door inside the one before.

The first door · Withdrawing the sensesPratyahara

Sights, sounds and itches keep pouring into a chattering mind. At this door you stop following them out. The senses come home, the way a tortoise draws in its legs.

"The drawing in of the organs is by their giving up their own objects and taking the form of the mind-stuff, as it were."2.54

The second door · One pointDharana

Hold the mind on one thing: the breath, a mantra, a flame. It wanders off. You bring it back. Bringing it back is the practice.

"Dharana is holding the mind on to some particular object."3.1

The tortoise is the Bhagavad Gita's picture for this (2.58). The sutra lines on these pages are Vivekananda's translations, from Raja Yoga.

Four Doors Inward4 / 11

The last two doors open on their own, or not at all.

The third door · AbsorptionDhyana

One day you notice you haven't had to come back. No "inhale," no "exhale," no "I'm supposed to be meditating." Attention just flows, the way it does when you're in the zone.

"An unbroken flow of knowledge in that object is Dhyana."3.2

The fourth door · UnionSamadhi

The one who is meditating drops away. Only what you were resting on is left, shining. If you're lucky, the ego dissolves and there is just awareness, as wide as everything.

"When that, giving up all forms, reflects only the meaning, it is Samadhi."3.3

You can't force these two. You keep showing up at the first two, and one day they open.

Four Doors Inward5 / 11

At the far end, a rain cloud.

Patanjali's last samadhi is called dharma-megha, the rain cloud of dharma. It comes to the one who wants nothing from it, not even enlightenment. After it, the kleshas fall away, and so does the karma that binds you.

One translation says it comes to someone no longer "anxious even concerning enlightenment."

Yoga Sutras 4.29–4.30, in Swami Veda Bharati's translation. The kleshas are the five knots of chapter 7. Teachers map the stages of samadhi before this one in different ways; I.K. Taimni's The Science of Yoga walks through them sutra by sutra.

The Science of YogaI. K. TaimniBook ↗

But I'm sure I've reached places along this path that have been very rewarding.

You already have every tool you need to start.

Practise with a new aim. Draw the senses in, bring the mind to one point, and let it be absorbed.

Four Doors Inward7 / 11

Jñāna is like letting muddy water settle.

People ask me for the process. There's no recipe where A, B and C make D. You stop stirring, and the water clears in its own time. There is an old map of how it goes, though.

VivekaDiscernment. Telling what's real and lasting (the Self) from what passes (the ego and the world).
VairagyaDetachment. Seeing that the world is fleeting, and loosening your grip on it.
ShatsampatSix virtues. Calm, self-control, withdrawing from the senses, endurance, faith in the teaching, and focus.
MumukshutvaLonging for freedom. Wanting liberation more than you want anything else.

Every chapter so far has been part of this. Living in the now (chapter 5) trains discernment. Untying the five knots (chapter 7) loosens your grip. The Basics (chapters 2 to 4) and the grooves you carve (chapter 6) build the six virtues and settle your nerves.

Four Doors Inward8 / 11

Everything so far was the walk to base camp.

The Basics, the breath, the grooves, the knots, the suit, the sliver, the stars: all of it gets you to the foot of the mountain. I'm telling you the mountain is there, and what you're looking for is at the top. Clouds may hide it. You may not believe me.

And there are no Sherpas on this climb. I can't carry you up. All I can do is point. Only you can climb it, one step at a time.

When pain, misery, or anger happen, it is time to look within you, not around you.Sadhguru · Inner Engineering

Four Doors Inward9 / 11

Right samadhi

Don't make meditation another escape.

Stillness can become one more place to hide, the way a drink or a feed can. That's dvesha, the knot of avoidance, wearing a meditation cushion. Right samadhi takes the middle path. You go in so you can come back, and live out here a little better. The last movement of this book is about the coming back.

Right samadhi is the last step of the Buddha's eightfold path. This lesson comes from a short meditation on it by Samaneri Jayasara, a Theravada nun in the Thai Forest tradition who lives in rural New South Wales.

Go in. Come back. Bring something with you.

Four Doors Inward10 / 11

Practice

Awareness meditation

  1. Sit comfortably. Close your eyes, or rest them on the floor.
  2. Let sounds come and go. Don't name them or follow them.
  3. Let sensations come and go: pressure, warmth, an itch.
  4. Let thoughts come and go too. You don't have to stop them.
  5. Notice what all of it shows up in. Sounds, feelings and thoughts arrive and leave. The noticing stays.
  6. Rest as that. When a thought carries you off, notice, and rest again.
  7. Ten minutes. Then open your eyes and take it into the next thing you do.

I learned this with Ram Dass's guided meditation "Awareness," about 17 minutes long, with music by Boreta and Superposition. It's a good guide for the first few times.

Let the monkey jump. You're the room it jumps in.

That's the end of the third movement. You've gone in. Now comes the harder part, the one most books skip: coming back out, into a life with jobs, kids, hockey games and dishes, and staying free in the middle of it.

Win or Lose

The last movement: coming back to live out here. It starts with what you're still holding. Letting go of the losses turns out to be the easy part.

Win or Lose1 / 10

Attachment is whatever you can't put down.

It doesn't matter what it is. For as long as you want to hold on to it, it will cause you suffering. That's just the way it works. This is raga, the third knot from chapter 7, and this chapter is about what it looks like in an ordinary week.

And there's always more to hold. Western society runs on a never-ending supply of new stuff, labels, opinions, outrages and flexes. The ego needs them to feel like it means something, so we juggle far too much.

The first thing my Hindu teacher wrote on his slate in teaching me was the statement, “Desire is a trap; desirelessness is moksha, or liberation; desire is the creator, desire is the destroyer, desire is the universe.”Ram Dass · Here We All Are, 1969
Win or Lose2 / 10

Freedom is always scheduled for some later date.

When I retire.

When I finally get the house. The car. The partner.

When I have time.

Freedomwhen I retire

The wheel rolls. The sign stays exactly as far away as it was.

Underneath all of them runs the ego's favourite question, "What's in it for me?" Every answer promises to be the last stop. Then the wheel turns, and the prize is still hanging just out in front.

In yoga this wheel is called samsara. However far it rolls, it never gets where it promised to go. I rode it for years, back in chapter 1, checking off goals and finding each one was one more thing to carry.

That's an idea worth giving up. Everything you need is right here, right now.

The work is yours. The fruit never was.

Find full reward
Of doing right in right! Let right deeds be
Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.

In good or evil: equability

Do the work. Let the result go. Stay even either way. That evenness, Krishna says, is yoga.

Eknath Easwaran's modern translation, the one I recommend, opens the verse: "You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work."

Win or Lose4 / 10

82 games a year, and I let every one of them set my mood

One made-up season, game by game. Marigold is a win, red is a loss.

For years, part of me was attached to how the Edmonton Oilers did. A win felt great. A loss felt awful. I carried it into the next day, sometimes longer, and into how I was with people, my family included.

I had no control over any of it. There are 32 teams and one Cup, so winning it all is the outlier. I still signed up for that suffering 82 times a year, and more in the playoffs.

I still love the game. Win or lose, it doesn't touch my mood anymore.

I get to watch some of the best athletes in the world play an entertaining game. Why spoil it by needing a result? In my mind we've already won everything and lost everything. All that's left is the moment.

Win or Lose5 / 10

Once you see it, you can't unsee it.

Every attachment is like the hockey. We fool ourselves that we have more control the closer it gets to home: the job, the kids, the plans for the weekend. Sit with it long enough, and that turns out to be an illusion too. Chapter 8 asked who was really deciding. The same answer applies here.

The comedian and activist Dick Gregory talked about the day the universe picks you.

What's dangerous is when the universe picks you and you put on the magic glasses. There are rules that go with them. You can never take them off. You never see things as they are supposed to be, you see things as they are. You cannot force anyone to wear them.Dick Gregory (1932–2017)
Win or Lose6 / 10

Here's the catch: you give up the upside too.

Non-attachment is a strange thing in practice. You don't only let go of the losses. You let go of the wins, and that can feel like losing meaning, purpose, direction, goals.

Some people call this the dark night of the soul, or decide they've had an ego death. I think mostly it's the old attachments losing their pull. They don't satisfy the way they used to. If you hit this stretch, check the Basics first. Flat and unmotivated can also just mean tired. Then give it time. What comes back in place of the old pull is quieter, and it lasts.

Will a rose smell as sweet? It does, and it doesn't.

Triumph and Disaster, those two impostors, and the one to watch

Triumph is the sneakier one. It's the upside that feels earned after all that hard work, the fruit of the action. It's the attachment we hold tightest.

If you've been reading this chapter as permission to stop caring, read this page twice. Watch a hummingbird feed. Its wings are a blur, and its head holds almost still at the flower. That's the picture: full effort, still centre.

Work hard all day. Then, at night, put it down.

Practice

Put it down tonight

A couple of years ago I sat in a satsang, a spiritual gathering, with Yogrishi Vishvketu (Vishva-ji). He suggested something like this.

  1. Before bed, write down what didn't get done today. All of it.
  2. Read it once. You'll pick it up again in the morning.
  3. Give yourself permission to put it down for the night: the to-dos, the goals, the commitments.
  4. Picture it in a bag by the door, waiting for you.
  5. If something floats back up, notice it, and set it down again.

It helps most on the nights sleep won't come. Give yourself permission, even if it's only for seven hours of rest. Sleep is the lever the others lean on, and this is one way to pull it.

Your page

Saved only on this device.

It will all be here in the morning.

So you put the results down. What do you pick up instead? The work itself. That's the next chapter, and it's the second of the three paths from chapter 1.

Chapter 13

Chop Wood, Carry Water

“Though a man may wish to live a hundred years, performing works, it will be thus with him; but not in any other way: work will thus not cling to a man.”

Isha Upanishad, verse 2 · tr. Max Müller, 1879

Chop Wood, Carry Water1 / 10

A warrior sits down in his chariot and can't go on.

This chapter is the Gita's second path, karma yoga, the one for doers. It starts with a man frozen. The Bhagavad Gita opens on a battlefield, Kurukshetra. Arjuna, a great warrior prince, asks to be driven out between the two armies. Across the field he sees cousins, friends and the elders who taught him.

Sorrow and compassion overwhelm him. He can't tell what's right anymore. He puts down his bow and sits. If you've ever frozen at the top of a to-do list, or in a parking lot before a hard day, you've sat where Arjuna sat.

His charioteer is Krishna, the divine in human form. The rest of the Gita is their conversation, right there between the armies.

Many readers, Gandhi among them, take the battle as allegory. Gandhi saw in it “the duel that perpetually went on in the hearts of mankind.” Krishna is drawn here only as a peacock feather.

Chop Wood, Carry Water2 / 10

Krishna's answer is karma yoga: get up and do the work.

Karma means action. Karma yoga is the yoga of selfless action. You do what's yours to do, fully, and let go of how it turns out. Success or failure. Praise or blame. You act from duty and love, and offer the results to the divine, or to the greater good. It's the "do the work" lever from chapter 3 and the letting go from chapter 12, joined into one path.

Thy right is to work only, but never with its fruits; let not the fruits of action be thy motive, nor let thy attachment be to inaction.Bhagavad Gita 2.47 · tr. Swami Swarupananda, 1909

The last clause is the warning. Letting go of the fruit is no excuse for doing nothing. For an anxious mind, that's the half worth underlining.

The Gita is a 700-verse poem inside the Mahabharata. An old verse calls it the milk of the Upanishads, the philosophical texts that close the Vedas. If you want to start reading, I recommend Eknath Easwaran's translation. The audiobook is a good way in.

Chop Wood, Carry Water3 / 10

Everyone is a stone in the arch, and every stone is holding something up.

Krishna explains with dharma. The word comes from a Sanskrit root meaning to hold or support. It means duty, path, the right order of things. Svadharma is your own piece of it, the work that's yours because of who and where you are.

Arjuna was a Kshatriya, born to the warrior class, so his duty was to fight a just war. Walking away would have left a gap in the arch. It would also have taught him to avoid.

Most of what anxiety makes us avoid is nowhere near as hard as war. Maybe you serve in the military, and that is your path. For most of us the field is smaller: a phone call, an inbox, a hard conversation.

The Gita's own version: better your own dharma done imperfectly than someone else's done well (3.35, paraphrased).

Chop Wood, Carry Water4 / 10

So how do you practise it on a Tuesday?

I lean on five foundations. They aren't steps in order. They're five ways to check whether the thing you're doing is karma yoga or just more hustle.

  • IntentionAct from love, compassion and duty. Leave gain out of it.
  • DetachmentLet go of the outcome. You can still care and still aim high. Your peace stops riding on the result.
  • DedicationOffer every act, however small. Even the dishes become worship.
  • DiscernmentSome actions are right and some aren't. Your gut usually knows which ones serve your path. When it doesn't, ask a teacher.
  • SelflessnessServe the good of all. The ego gets smaller, and the connections get easier to see.
Chop Wood, Carry Water5 / 10
Duty alone. Friction all the way.
Duty is seldom sweet. It is only when love greases its wheels that it runs smoothly; it is a continuous friction otherwise. How else could parents do their duties to their children, husbands to their wives, and vice versa? Do we not meet with cases of friction every day in our lives? Duty is sweet only through love, and love shines in freedom alone. Yet is it freedom to be a slave to the senses, to anger, to jealousies and a hundred other petty things that must occur every day in human life? In all these little roughnesses that we meet with in life, the highest expression of freedom is to forbear.Swami Vivekananda · Karma-Yoga, “What Is Duty?”, 1896

Forbear. I'd go one step further. Love your fate.

Amor fati.

Latin for “love of fate.” The phrase is Nietzsche's, from The Gay Science (1882). The idea is older. The Stoic Epictetus told his students to want things “to happen as they do happen.”

The Gay ScienceFriedrich NietzscheBook ↗Audiobook ↗
Chop Wood, Carry Water6 / 10

It clicked for me in my marriage.

There were things that mattered to my wife that I didn't hear, see or feel until I started looking for the work, outside my ego and my wants.

What I found was a list of Basics for my marriage, like the Basics for anxiety in the first movement of this book. Plain, unglamorous things, done every day. They let us work in tandem more often than at odds. And when one of us is short-tempered, the most generous interpretation from chapter 3 nearly always holds: somebody is tired, or hungry, or has had no time alone. Good habits grow with a good partner.

So I have a duty as a husband, and I do it without expecting anything back.

It has been rewarding. What matters is that I keep practising, and don't rest on any fruit it bears.

On a two-person saw, each of you pulls in turn.

Chop Wood, Carry Water7 / 10

Before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water.

After enlightenment, chop wood, carry water.

Everything you need to be happy is in front of you before thought arises. Once you see that, there's nothing left to do but get on with the work.

In a modern house and a marriage, it might go: wash the dishes, help with the meals, do the laundry.

It's usually called a Zen koan, but this wording is modern and has no known classical source. Its roots are real. The Chinese layman Pang Yun (740–808) wrote that his miraculous power was hauling water and carrying firewood.

Chop Wood, Carry Water8 / 10

There's no manual for being a dad, so I use the five.

Each kid is so different that every day is a fresh chance to practise all five foundations.

Intention.Act out of love and compassion.
Detachment.From whatever I expected of the day.
Dedication.There's always something to pick up. As a parent you never run out, literally or figuratively.
Discernment.Is this the right thing to do?
Selflessness.Which is so much of being a good parent anyway.

The same goes for your job, your friendships and your learning. Find your duty, pick up the work, and expect nothing in return.

Chop Wood, Carry Water9 / 10

Practice

One chore as an offering

  1. Pick one chore today, one you'd usually rush or resent. The dishes, the laundry, the lunches.
  2. Before you start, decide who it's for. Your family, your partner, a stranger, or the work itself.
  3. Do it with full attention. The heat of the water. The weight of each plate. The sound it makes.
  4. When the mind starts keeping score (who did it last, whether anyone will notice), see it, and come back to the next plate.
  5. When it's done, offer it. Let it go without needing a thank-you.

Before enlightenment, the dishes.After enlightenment, the dishes.

One knot is left, the fifth one, and I've saved it for last on purpose. It's the one underneath all the others.

Chapter 14

The Second Life

We saved the heaviest subject for last, because you needed the Basics and a settled mind before you could look at it.

The Second Life1 / 10

The last knot is the one under all the others.

Patanjali names five knots (chapter 7). The fifth is abhinivesha, the clinging to life. Turn it over and you find the fear of death. He says even the wise carry it. Pull on any anxious thought hard enough, the heart that's racing, the job that might go, the child who's late home, and this is the knot you reach.

Flowing through its own nature, and established even in the learned, is the clinging to life.Patanjali, Yoga Sutras 2.9 · tr. Swami Vivekananda, 1896

This book left this knot for the end, because it weighs a lot when anxiety is loud. If today isn't the day, skip to the practice. These pages will keep.

The Second Life2 / 10

Die before you die, and find out what's left.

Death is a stripping away of all that is not you. The secret of life is to “die before you die”—and find that there is no death.Eckhart Tolle · The Power of Now

A cicada climbs out of the ground after dark, grips a stem and splits its old skin down the back. Before dawn it has walked out. The empty shell stays behind, still holding on.

Most of what we're afraid to lose is shell. The name, the badges, what people think of us. That's the spacesuit from chapter 8, seen from the end of its life. You can step out of it while you're still alive, and what steps out is the awareness that has been watching all along.

“Die before you die” is far older than Tolle. It's a Sufi saying, often credited to the Prophet Muhammad, though hadith scholars say it isn't one of his. In Japanese, utsusemi means both the empty cicada shell and this passing world.

The Power of NowEckhart TolleBook ↗Audiobook ↗
The Second Life3 / 10

At every funeral, I sat in the back row and left early.

At every funeral I went to, I sat at the back, left as soon as I could and cried all the way home in the car. If there was a chance to speak, I always wanted to share a story. The lump in my throat always won. That was dvesha, the knot of avoidance, and the fence moving in a little each time.

I spoke once, at my grandma's funeral, when I was 12. I was a bawling mess.

That was before I'd looked at my own death and accepted it.

The Second Life4 / 10

We have two lives, and most of us are still in the first.

The second begins when you realize you only have one.

Alan Watts liked to ask his listeners to imagine their own death, really imagine it. When I finally did, it worked like fertilizer. What grew out of it was a decision. I wasn't going to let other people's judgments, or my own mind, stop me from living.

For my 40th birthday I threw a party and gave myself permission to set the spacesuit down completely (chapter 8). I lived in bliss for the better part of a year.

The two-lives line is usually credited to Confucius. It isn't his. It's best known as the title of Raphaëlle Giordano's 2015 French novel, Ta deuxième vie commence quand tu comprends que tu n'en as qu'une.

Your Second Life Begins When You Realize You Only Have OneRaphaëlle GiordanoBook ↗
The Second Life5 / 10

But life is real, and it tested all of this.

A philosophy has to be tested before you can trust it.

I watched our health-care system fail my wife's mom, and I did my best to hold my wife up. Her mom died at 63.

My wife's strength, and our ability to stay mindful, got us through. I kept going to the yoga studio with a heavy heart, grateful that nobody talks much there. If anyone had said more than hi, I might have come apart. I kept the Basics going too, badly some days, because grief is tired and hungry and overwhelmed all at once, and the alarm knows it.

The practice held.

The Second Life6 / 10

My mentor was an umbrella for a lot of people.

From a young age, my mentor sheltered a lot of people. Even now that he's gone, his philanthropy still does.

Alzheimer's took him slowly. Near the end, the strongest person I've ever known needed the kind of care he had spent his life giving. We gave it gladly, and it was still hard.

The Second Life7 / 10

His celebration of life

  • I was master of ceremonies.
  • I gave the eulogy.
  • I wrote the obituary.
  • I made the video of his life in photos,
  • the program, the images on the screen.

And this time, I knew just what to do.

Back in chapter 5, in Kathmandu, Bhagavan Das made Ram Dass a promise: “If you can be here now, when then is now, you will have super-consciousness and super-energy and you will know just what to do.” I said I'd tell you how I found out it was true. This is how.

I went from not being able to speak at a funeral to giving him a send-off anyone would be proud of. We had talked about what he wanted 25 years before. Every skill I'd picked up since was there when I needed it. Super consciousness and super energy. None of it came from trying harder. It came from everything in this book, done for long enough that it was there when the day arrived: a settled body, a mind that stayed in the room, and no spacesuit left to protect.

When it was over, I felt I'd fulfilled one of my purposes on this planet.

The Second Life8 / 10

He isn't gone. He's in this book.

I see the echo of his life in his kids and his grandkids. He's in this book, too. He taught me the Paradoxical Commandments. He taught me to act and learn, don't debate and wait. He told his own version of the two wolves.

We're meant to go through all of it. Life without death would be a universe with no birth and no rebirth. And the ever-shining Self, the part of you that watches, has a front-row seat for this remarkable display that is life.

Don't fear death. Fear not living this one fully.

The Second Life9 / 10

Practice

Yoga nidra: the rehearsal

Yogic sleep. You lie in savasana, the corpse pose, and rest deeply while staying awake. The name of the pose isn't an accident. You practise setting the whole suit down, and finding that the awareness stays. Give it twenty minutes or so. It also happens to be one of the best things I know for the sleep lever, so it belongs to the Basics as much as to this chapter.

  1. Lie on your back. A pillow under your knees and a blanket, if you like. Let the floor take your weight.
  2. Set a sankalpa, one short sentence in the present tense, like “I am loving awareness.” Say it silently three times.
  3. Move your attention through the body, one part at a time. Right thumb, each finger, palm, wrist, elbow, shoulder, then down the right side to the toes. Then the left side. Just visit each place.
  4. Feel the breath rise and fall in your belly. Count breaths backward if it helps. If you lose count, start again.
  5. Let the counting go too. Rest, awake, with nothing to do.
  6. Say your sankalpa three more times. Then notice the room, move your fingers and toes, roll onto your side and sit up slowly.

If lying still with your eyes closed stirs up panic, open your eyes or sit up. It still counts.

If you'd like a voice to guide you, I record yoga nidra on my podcast, Yoga with Wes.

Use this moment wisely.

That's the whole path, as I found it. Settle the body. Watch the mind. Find where you begin. Come back. When it gets hard, and it will, go back to the Basics and the long exhale, and start again from there. I've been down here before, and this is the way out I know.

The Companions

There are a thousand paths to the same place, and each of us has to walk our own. These are the teachers who kept me company on mine. Each one is drawn as an emblem.

Tap a number to go back to the chapters where they appear.

  • Ram Dass

    1931–2019

    Born Richard Alpert, a Harvard psychologist who went to India in 1967 and came home as Ram Dass. He called the body a spacesuit, something you put on at birth to live on this plane.

    Chapters0105081114

  • Dr. Claire Weekes

    1903–1990

    An Australian GP who had lived through anxiety herself, then spent her life writing to anxious people in plain words. Her method fits in four: face, accept, float, let time pass.

    Chapter02

  • Alan Watts

    1915–1973

    An English writer who moved to America in 1938 and explained Zen, Taoism and Hindu thought to Western listeners, much of it on the radio. His 1951 book The Wisdom of Insecurity is subtitled A Message for an Age of Anxiety.

    Chapters050814

  • Sam Harris

    Born 1967

    An American neuroscientist and writer who teaches meditation without the religion. In Waking Up (2014) he argues that the feeling of a self behind your eyes is an illusion. Go looking for it and you won't find anyone there.

    Chapters0508

  • Larry Anderson

    Edmonton · died 2024

    My uncle. He grew up in Ritchie playing in the Mill Creek Ravine, left home at sixteen, and went on to co-found Lincolnberg Homes and the ManCap Group, which built more than 8,000 homes for Alberta families. Then he spent decades giving it back, most of all to young people trying to find their way. He wrote two books, Wisdom to Live Your Magic and Inspiration to Live Your Magic.

    He was a bridge builder, in the spirit of Will Allen Dromgoole's poem, and the first person to believe in me beyond what was evident.

    “This chasm, that has been naught to me,
    To that fair-haired youth may a pitfall be.
    He, too, must cross in the twilight dim;
    Good friend, I am building the bridge for him.”

    Will Allen Dromgoole, “The Bridge Builder,” 1900

Music: “A Little Powder” by Blue Dot Sessions (sessions.blue), licensed under Creative Commons BY-NC 4.0. The chimes, bowls and breaths are made in the page itself.

At the back1 / 6

The Companions

  • The Stoics

    Seneca, c. 4 BCE–65 CE · Epictetus, c. 50–135 · Marcus Aurelius, 121–180

    A statesman who wrote letters to a worried friend, a freed slave who taught, and an emperor who wrote notes to himself. Marcus told himself to be like a headland: the waves keep breaking, it stands, and the water around it settles.

    Chapters010513

  • Patanjali

    Dates unknown

    Nobody knows when he lived. Guesses run from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. His Yoga Sutras lay out the whole path in 196 short lines, the eight limbs among them. Sūtra means thread.

    Chapters0406071114

  • Swami Vivekananda

    1863–1902

    An Indian monk, Ramakrishna's chief disciple, who carried yoga and Vedanta to the West, starting in Chicago in 1893. He compared the mind to a monkey: restless, then drunk, then stung by a scorpion.

    Chapters01060711121314

  • Samaneri Jayasara

    Living, in New South Wales

    A Buddhist nun in the Thai Forest Theravada tradition who lives in a hermitage in rural New South Wales. She records readings of teachers from many traditions, from the Buddha to Ramana Maharshi, and posts them on YouTube.

    Chapter11

Take good ideas from anywhere, and from anyone.

A poem

If—

Rudyard Kipling · 1910

If you can keep your head when all about you Are losing theirs and blaming it on you, If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you, But make allowance for their doubting too; If you can wait and not be tired by waiting, Or being lied about, don’t deal in lies, Or being hated, don’t give way to hating, And yet don’t look too good, nor talk too wise:

If you can dream—and not make dreams your master; If you can think—and not make thoughts your aim; If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster And treat those two impostors just the same; If you can bear to hear the truth you’ve spoken Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools, Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken, And stoop and build ’em up with worn-out tools:

If you can make one heap of all your winnings And risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss, And lose, and start again at your beginnings And never breathe a word about your loss; If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew To serve your turn long after they are gone, And so hold on when there is nothing in you Except the Will which says to them: ‘Hold on!’

If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue, Or walk with Kings—nor lose the common touch, If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you, If all men count with you, but none too much; If you can fill the unforgiving minute With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run, Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it, And—which is more—you’ll be a Man, my son!

I first met this poem in a talk Charlie Munger gave at the University of Michigan in 2010. When I read it aloud, the last line becomes “you’ll be an adult, my child.”

First published in Rewards and Fairies (1910), after the story “Brother Square-Toes.” The text above is Kipling’s own.

About the author

Wes Gunderson had anxiety for thirty-five years before he knew what it was called. He spent most of that time building things: a career that began in marketing and web development, then two decades in home building and finance with the Lincolnberg group, where he was VP Finance, a director and an operating partner, and ran a sixty-million-dollar-a-year home building operation. He checked everything off the list. None of it touched the anxiety.

At thirty-nine a Ram Dass recording opened a door, and he walked through it the way he does everything, all the way in: the Gita, the Yoga Sutras, Vivekananda, the breath, and finally yoga teacher training. He began teaching Yoga Nidra and running workshops on mindfulness and meditation for anxiety, the course this book grew out of. He hosts the Yoga with Wes podcast and still practises every day, imperfectly.

Today he chairs Gunderson Capital Corp., an investing and advisory firm, and builds small software for small businesses on the side. He lives in Edmonton, Alberta, with Alison and their boys, Will, Matt and Winston. He is not a doctor or a therapist, and this book is not a substitute for either. He made it free because the things in it were given to him freely, by teachers and by friends who jumped in the hole.

Proof notes for Wes

What changed, chapter by chapter

Every fact-check, correction and cut against the workshop drafts, with where each chapter's material came from. Strip this section before publishing.

01 I've Been Down Here Before

From: W1 intro, Qualifications, What is Jñāna · W2 opening story

  • "In this excerpt, a recovered alcoholic offers words of wisdom to a friend struggling with alcoholism"Now: Leo McGarry, a recovering alcoholic, tells the story to Josh Lyman, who is struggling after being shot. The episode is about Josh's post-traumatic stress, which fits this book even better. Credited to The West Wing, "Noël" (season 2, aired December 13, 2000), teleplay by Aaron Sorkin from a story by Peter Parnell.
  • The whole hole monologue quoted from The West WingNow: retold in your words. Only the friend's last line is quoted, and it's credited.
  • "The Latin equivalent of Jñāna is Gnosis"Now: gnosis is Greek. Jñāna, gnosis and English know share one ancient root.
  • Ramakrishna: "One who has merely heard of fire has ajnana… seen fire has jnana… built a fire and cooked on it has vijnana" as a direct quoteNow: paraphrased, with a footnote. The fire wording is a popular retelling. In The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna he makes the point with milk (heard of it, seen it, drunk it) and with fire hidden in wood that you then cook rice on.
  • Ram Dass called jñāna "the yoga of the mind beating out the mind"Now: used as your own line, without quotation marks. I couldn't find Ram Dass saying it in print. The closest is his line about using the mind "exquisitely in order to get free of the trap that you got caught in" (ramdass.org).
  • "In 2019 East Forest released a collaborative album with Ram Dass and my algorithm served me the track I am Loving Awareness"Now: kept, with the names pinned down in a footnote. The album is Ram Dass by East Forest, released in full in August 2019. "I Am Loving Awareness," with Krishna Das, came out first, in January 2019. It's a track, not the album title.
  • "for many years they experimented with LSD legally, until they got kicked out of Harvard and spent a few more years continuing the experiments illegally, before going broke and their separate ways"Now: he and Timothy Leary researched psychedelics until Harvard dismissed them both in 1963. I cut the later years because I couldn't confirm "illegally" or "broke," and this page doesn't need them.
  • "a guru named Maharaji, which means Great King"Now: Neem Karoli Baba, known as Maharaj-ji, who gave him the name Ram Dass, "servant of God."
  • "this old guy that 'loved his wheelchair'"Now: kept as your impression, without quotation marks: "an old man who seemed to love his wheelchair." Ram Dass did call the 1997 stroke "a gift in many ways" (Tricycle), and the timeline page says so.
  • Ram Dass "influenced and inspired many people like Steve Jobs and Wayne Dyer" (Draft)Now: cut.
  • Krishna's warning in Gita 18.67 (Easwaran's translation), "forbidden knowledge," and "worth offending Krishna"Now: cut. The page keeps the plain point that teachers rarely start students on jñāna, and why you start there anyway.
  • "the anxious mind is leading to something call Apara (Lower) Samskara/Vasana, rather Para (Supreme)… like watching people drive the wrong way down a one-way street"Now: the one-way street stays. The Sanskrit terms are dropped here, because samskara and vasana get chapter 6.
  • Vivekananda's Jnana Yoga and its first chapter, "The Necessity of Religion"Now: cut. Vivekananda gets one footnote, at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago.
  • The roll call of teachers (Weekes, Ram Dass, Watts, Vivekananda, Samaneri Jayasara, Sam Harris, the Stoics, Larry Anderson) and Dzogchen's TrekchöNow: cut from this chapter. The teachers appear as emblems in The Companions at the back. Dzogchen keeps one mention on the "Before we start" page.
  • "I am not a Doctor, Therapist, Psychologist, or even a certified yoga teacher (yet)"Now: "I'm not a doctor, a therapist or a psychologist." I dropped the yoga-teacher line until you tell me where it stands.
  • "enough trauma to make everyone in this room cry"Now: "enough trauma to make a room full of people cry."
  • Class logistics: Tania, Leala, the Prana studio, the 45-minute talk and 30-minute practice, notes by email, "sufficiently warned"Now: cut. The warning survives as "If a page unsettles you, skip it, or put the book down for a while. I won't be offended."

  • The drafts recommend a sankalpa but never describe how Ram Dass used "I am loving awareness"Now: the practice is built from Ram Dass's own description on ramdass.org: attention in the middle of the chest, the spiritual heart; a few deep breaths, breathing love in and out; the phrase; loving whatever awareness touches. Your "about a month" closes it.

02 The Alarm

From: W1 Understanding Anxiety

  • Claire Weekes, "an Australian psychiatrist"Now: an Australian GP. She qualified in medicine at 42 in 1945 and never trained as a psychiatrist.
  • Her definition of sensitization set as a direct quoteNow: paraphrased. I couldn't match the exact wording to her book, so check it against your copy before quoting her.
  • "Floating" as her whole methodNow: her four words in full: face, accept, float, let time pass.
  • Fight, flight, freeze, fawn, flop, uncreditedNow: "fawn" credited to Pete Walker, who named it.
  • The heart-attack spiral ending in "just anxiety"Now: adds that chest pain deserves a doctor the first time. "Just anxiety" should be a doctor's conclusion, not the book's.
  • Weekes as a credentialNow: her own story. She was misdiagnosed with tuberculosis at 26 and spent two years anxious, the same "been down here before" move as chapter 1.
03 The Levers

From: W1 The Basics

  • "A 2018 study showed that drinking water was associated with a decrease in anxiety and depression."Now: the study is a one-time survey of 3,327 Iranian adults. Drinking fewer than two glasses a day was linked to more depression. The anxiety link pointed the same way but wasn't significant once other factors were adjusted for, and a survey can't show cause.
  • The sleep study set as a quote: "sleep deprivation amplified reactions in the amygdala and anterior insula ... strongest in people who displayed high levels of trait anxiety"Now: paraphrased from the paper itself (Goldstein et al., J Neurosci 2013): 18 healthy young adults, one night without sleep. The quoted wording isn't the paper's, and trait anxiety predicted the jump in the anterior insula only, not the amygdala.
  • "Minimum 7 hours a night is recommend"Now: credited to the 2015 consensus of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society (seven or more hours for adults).
  • "More than 400 milligrams of caffeine per day (around four to five cups of coffee) may increase the likelihood of anxiety and panic attacks in people sensitive to it, according to the U.S. Food & Drug Administration."Now: the FDA's current wording: 400 mg a day is "not generally associated with negative effects" for most adults, and it now equates that to two to three 12-ounce cups of coffee. It lists anxiety and jitters among the signs of too much, says sensitivity varies widely, and doesn't mention panic attacks.
  • "caffeine-induced anxiety disorder" is "a subclass in the DSM-5"Now: a type of substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder in the DSM-5.
  • "Alcohol is a stimulant and depressant ... GABA is released ... long term, alcohol use can create a GABA depletion ... and increase the risk of panic attacks"Now: alcohol boosts GABA's braking effect, and with regular drinking the brain adapts by easing off its own brakes, so the alarm rebounds as the alcohol wears off. "GABA depletion" and the panic-attack claim are softened to that rebound; the dehydration point is dropped.
  • "it is recommended you discuss this option with a doctor if you have a strong dependence on alcohol"Now: moved into the body text and made plain: if you drink every day, talk to a doctor before you stop, because withdrawal can bring seizures and can be life-threatening.
  • The exercise study set as a quoteNow: paraphrased with its numbers (Aylett, Small & Bower 2018: 15 trials, 675 patients, compared with waiting-list controls), plus a line to check with a doctor first if you have a heart condition.
  • CBT "is leaning into that which makes you anxious; studies show 'strong support for both the efficacy and effectiveness of CBT as an acute intervention for adult anxiety disorders'"Now: paraphrased. I couldn't find that exact sentence in any paper I could open. The closest is Otte (2011): CBT "demonstrates both efficacy in randomized controlled trials and effectiveness in naturalistic settings." Leaning into what scares you is exposure, the core of CBT for anxiety, so the page says that.
  • "There is a Latin phrase Fati Amor"Now: amor fati, the phrase Nietzsche made famous (The Gay Science §276, 1882; Ecce Homo).
  • "Michael Jordan missed 9000 shots and lost over 300 games including 26 games where he missed a game wining shot"Now: matched to the 1997 Nike "Failure" ad: more than 9,000 shots, almost 300 games lost, and 26 times trusted with the game-winning shot and missed. Two sentences of the ad are quoted.
  • "I read or heard of a study that (I can't track down but essentially) showed humans are more successful at filling, administering, and completing veterinary prescriptions for their pets"Now: credited to Jordan Peterson's 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 2, where it appears without a study. The footnote says no study seems to have measured it and that pet owners miss doses too (a 2013 YouGov survey of dog owners; a study of cat owners in which 39% didn't give medication as prescribed).
  • "The espresso would be dehydrating"Now: the shots took the place of water. I kept the loop to what happened. Whether coffee itself dehydrates regular drinkers is disputed, and I couldn't check it this round.
  • "Possibly exploring your dosha type under Ayurvedic diet"Now: cut. It opens a big subject with no evidence behind it for anxiety.
  • The section's epigraph: "yoga chitta vritti nirodha" (Yoga Sutra 1.2)Now: cut from this chapter, which starts straight from the body.
  • "Quiet the Mind" and "Control the breath" as levers, with the 2018 breath reviewNow: pointed forward on the feed page, since chapter 4 is the breath. The 2010 mindfulness review is kept as a footnote with its real numbers (39 studies, 1,140 people); the breath review is left for chapter 4.
  • "The two things I would add to the Basics": a sadhana and a sankalpa, with the East Forest storyNow: left out of this chapter. The sankalpa story belongs with chapter 1's "I am loving awareness."

Still to decide

  • The espresso spiral: how long did it run, and what did the crash look like? One concrete detail (a number of shots a day, a day you couldn't get up) would make page 6 land harder.
  • Peterson is a lightning rod for some readers. Keep the pets line with his name in the footnote, or drop it and let the 8-and-80 idea stand on its own?
  • I cut the Ayurvedic dosha suggestion from the food lever. Do you want it back as a one-line pointer?

04 The Long Exhale

From: W2 Breath Work · W3 Wizard of Ah · Draft (box, 4-7-8)

  • Opening epigraph: five sentences from James Nestor's Breath ("The most efficient breathing rhythm occurred when ... I have seen patients transformed by adopting regular breathing practices.")Now: cut and paraphrased as "James Nestor puts the sweet spot at five and a half breaths a minute." The quote is long for an in-copyright book, and its last sentence is someone else's words that Nestor is quoting.
  • "The ideal breath according to studies is 5.5 seconds in and 5.5 seconds out; which corresponds to ... the rosary or kirtan"Now: the rosary study (Bernardi and colleagues, BMJ 2001) found about six breaths a minute, for the Ave Maria in Latin and for a yoga mantra. Kirtan wasn't studied. Five and a half is credited to Nestor.
  • These traditions "evolving to fit a niche, a peace niche"Now: framed as the study authors' own guess: the rosary and mantras may have caught on partly because they slow the breath to this rhythm.
  • "One of the evolutionary results of cooking food is that Sapiens needed to chew their food much less"Now: Nestor's full sequence: cooking, then farming, then soft processed food in the last 300 years. In an NPR interview he puts most of the blame on the recent part ("it's chewing"), so the page leads with chewing and the jaw.
  • "Our ancestors would spend hours breaking down fibers chewing every day"Now: a number: a primate our size would be expected to spend about 48% of its active day feeding; we spend about 4.7% (Organ and colleagues, PNAS 2011).
  • "Our brains were evolving to be bigger and bigger crowding the nasal cavity as well"Now: cut. It's in Nestor's story, but the page sticks to chewing and jaws, the part with skull evidence behind it (von Cramon-Taubadel, PNAS 2011).
  • Mouth breathing "increases bacteria in your system (due to a lack of filtration)"Now: cut. Nestor's bacteria point is about blocked noses. The page says only that the mouth skips the nose's filtering.
  • "If you don't use it, you lose it": mouth breathing shrinks the nasal cavity, "another negative feedback loop"Now: cut; I couldn't find support beyond Nestor's own experiment. Added a plain note that a nose that's blocked most of the time is worth a doctor's visit.
  • Air through the nose is "slowed down, filtered, humidified and conditioned," quoted from a Nestor podcastNow: stated as plain anatomy without quote marks (slowed, filtered, warmed and moistened, by the turbinates). I couldn't find those exact words from Nestor.
  • "LONGER EXHALES activate the Parasympathetic Nervous System through the Vagus nerve" ... "you can force a parasympathetic response"Now: drawn as the real mechanism: the pulse quickens on the in-breath and slows on the out-breath (respiratory sinus arrhythmia), so a longer out-breath spends more time on the brake. "Force" is dropped. Slowing the breath does most of the work. One study found long exhales felt more relaxing than long inhales (Van Diest 2014), but a 2024 study found no extra heart-rate effect from a 1:2 ratio at six breaths a minute.
  • "A regular practise of longer exhale breath work can significantly reduce the onset, severity, and intensity of anxiety symptoms"Now: cut as a medical promise. The practice page keeps your line about the price of admission.
  • "Breath work is your most powerful weapon in your fight with anxiety"Now: "the most powerful tool you have." "Weapon" and "fight" clash with chapter 2's Weekes advice to stop fighting it.
  • Ujjayi "has been shown to increase oxygen levels"Now: cut. In the study I found (Mason and colleagues, 2013), plain slow breathing raised oxygen saturation just as much, and ujjayi gave a smaller baroreflex gain. Ujjayi stays as a way to stretch and hear the breath.
  • 4-7-8: "This practise can be done 6 to 8 times roughly in two minutes"; "a sure way to do this"Now: Weil's own guidance: no more than four breaths at a time for the first month, then up to eight, twice a day; count faster if the hold is hard, since the ratio matters more than the seconds. Added his tongue position and the whoosh. "A sure way" dropped.
  • Breath-hold caution given for box breathing onlyNow: repeated for 4-7-8, which also has a hold.
  • Box breathing "can bring balance, equilibrium, and equanimity"Now: "this one steadies you." Box breathing keeps in and out even, so the page says plainly that the next two pacers are the ones that lean on the brake.
  • "In the Rig Veda, the three sounds represent the three stages of cosmic creation: the Kalpa, the Manvantara and the Divya-Yuga"Now: cut. I couldn't find a source tying A, U and M to these three, and the page only needs the A.
  • "In the Tibetan tradition of Dzogchen, or Great Perfection, the sounds represent seed syllables of the Tibetan alphabet"; the three gunasNow: cut for one idea per page. In Dzogchen it's the single white A that matters, and that's what the page keeps.
  • The Radiance Sutras reading (a full paragraph of Lorin Roche's commentary, plus the jna augha mantra)Now: shortened to two quoted words, "a natural mantra," credited to Roche.
  • Practice: "20 minutes, twice a day" (notes) and "at least once a day" (homework)Now: "Twenty minutes, once a day. Twice if you can."
  • The session's opening sighing breathsNow: kept as the title-page instruction, and backed on page 10 by the 2023 Stanford study of exhale-heavy cyclic sighing (Balban and colleagues).

Still to decide

  • I couldn't see the text of The Radiance Sutras online. Please check that "a natural mantra" matches your copy before it goes out.
  • Is "Wizard of Ah" your own name for the practice? If it came from a teacher, I'll credit them.
  • The white A on page 10 is set in type with the reader's own Tibetan font (iPhone, Android, Mac and Windows all have one). Would you like someone who reads Tibetan to check it, or would you prefer a hand-drawn letter?
  • Your notes say twenty minutes twice a day; the homework said at least once. The practice page says once a day, twice if you can. Is that right?

Check before print

  • Lorin Roche's "a natural mantra" against Wes's copy of The Radiance Sutras.
  • The Tibetan letter A renders in the reader's own Tibetan font; worth one check on an older Android phone.

From: W3 Nowness Awareness

  • Ram Dass met the young man from Laguna Beach "in Tibet"Now: in Kathmandu, in 1967.
  • "a tall blonde 23-year-old from Laguna Beach"Now: "a very tall young American from Laguna Beach, California, who went by Bhagavan Das." He was born about 1945, so he was about 22, and the age is dropped.

09 The Sliver

From: W5 Nature of Consciousness

  • "Approximately 50% of brain processing power is dedicated to processing visual information"Now: vision gets more of the cortex than any other sense, roughly a fifth to a quarter of it (about 20% in Wandell's count, about 27% in Van Essen's). "About half" is the figure for macaque monkeys, which is likely where the 50% comes from.
  • Vision's processing power "is coming at the expense of our sense of smell"; "we are losing smell genes to make room for visual processing space"Now: cut. The idea that primates traded smell genes for colour vision (Gilad et al. 2004) wasn't supported by later work (Matsui, Go & Niimura 2010), and genes don't free up processing space.
  • Bluebottle butterfly "(15)" photoreceptorsNow: at least 15 kinds of light receptor in the common bluebottle (Graphium sarpedon), the most found in any insect; the researchers think about four of them do everyday colour vision.
  • Peacock mantis shrimp "(12-16)" photoreceptors, implying better colour visionNow: 12 kinds of colour receptor (8 for visible light, 4 for ultraviolet). Added the twist from Thoen et al. (2014): mantis shrimp are worse than people at telling close colours apart (they needed a 15 to 25 nm difference; people manage about 5).
  • Eagles "are said to have vision 4 to 5 times better than humans"Now: about 2.3 times as sharp. The wedge-tailed eagle resolves about 140 cycles per degree to our 60 (Caves et al. 2018). Its foveal cones are smaller (about 2 µm across to our 3).
  • Animals with echolocation "can hear up to 100,000 hertz such as the dolphins or bats"Now: dolphins and bats call far above human hearing, and some bats go past 200,000 (212 kHz is the highest bat call known). The dolphin's exact upper limit isn't given on the page.
  • Greater wax moth "can hear up to 300,000 hertz through hypersensitive hearing"Now: kept: hearing "approaching 300 kHz," the highest frequency sensitivity of any animal known (Moir, Jackson & Windmill 2013).
  • "We have something like 10,000 taste buds"Now: about 2,000 to 8,000, all in the mouth (Britannica). 10,000 is a popular figure at the high end.
  • Catfish "have something like 175,000 taste buds"Now: kept as the count for a big catfish, spread over its whole body. Popular sources give "more than 100,000" typically and "as many as 175,000" in large fish; I couldn't find the primary count.
  • Elephant "1,948 receptor genes (compared to 811 in dogs)"Now: kept, labelled as smell-receptor genes in the African elephant (Niimura et al. 2014), and added humans at about 400 (396).
  • The star-nosed mole "beats us in sense of touch because its touch receptors exceed ours"Now: about 25,000 touch organs (Eimer's organs) on a 22-ray star a little over a centimetre across, with five times as many touch nerve fibres as a whole human hand (Catania).
  • "An estimated 100 billion neurons"Now: about 86 billion (Azevedo et al. 2009). The 100 billion figure was never actually measured.
  • Each neuron "can make up to something like 1,000 connections"Now: thousands each (about 7,000 on average for a neocortical neuron).
  • "Your brain could store approximately 2.5 petabytes of data"Now: moved to a footnote and labelled as one rough 2010 estimate (Paul Reber in Scientific American, which assumed a billion neurons with a thousand connections each). "Nobody really knows."
  • 100 million songs × 3 minutes = "540 years"Now: about 570 years (300 million minutes is 5 million hours, or about 570 years). A footnote adds that Spotify's co-CEO put the catalogue at "something like 250 million" tracks in April 2026, which would take more than 1,400 years.
  • The Cognitive Bias Codex (180+ biases) and the six anxious-mind biases (catastrophizing, overgeneralization, mind reading, emotional reasoning, personalization, filtering)Now: moved to chapter 7. This chapter gives the filtering problem one page, built on the literal blind spot, and points to chapter 7.
  • "A 'hard problem' (David Chalmers on what it is like to be a..bat)"Now: the bat question is Thomas Nagel's ("What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", 1974). Chalmers named the hard problem of consciousness (a 1994 talk, published in 1995).
  • Seth's "controlled hallucination" explained as "the body does something and then the brain creates a story… the muscles seem to fire first"Now: described the way Seth uses it: perception is the brain's best guess about what's out there, kept in line by the senses. The timing experiments (Libet's) are a separate line of research; they found brain activity ahead of the felt decision, not muscles firing before neurons. They belong with free will in chapter 8.
  • Epigraph from Seth's Being You (three sentences: "It may seem as though the self… though of a very special kind.")Now: replaced with two short sentences from his TED2017 talk ("We're all hallucinating all the time, including right now. It's just that when we agree about our hallucinations, we call that reality."). The self-as-perception idea fits chapter 8 better.
  • Munger: "Any year that you don't destroy one of your best-loved ideas is probably a wasted year."Now: quoted as it appears in David Clark's Tao of Charlie Munger: "Any year that passes in which you don't destroy one of your best loved ideas is a wasted year."
  • The four "ultimate ideas" to destroy (doer or knower, separate from the universe, ego as the whole of you, getting a complete picture)Now: this chapter takes only the last one. The doer belongs to chapter 8 and separateness to chapter 10.
  • "Increase our vibrational level"; the Munger talk recommendation; the centipede, free will, Sapolsky, Harris and the Gita passageNow: cut here. The centipede and free will are in chapter 8; the Munger talk could go in Worth Your Time.

13 Chop Wood, Carry Water

From: Bonus Karma Yoga

  • “Fati Amor,” called “the stoic principle”Now: amor fati (Latin word order, “love of fate”). The phrase is Nietzsche's, from The Gay Science §276 (1882). The page links the idea to the Stoics through Epictetus (Handbook 8), who never used the phrase.
  • “There is a Zen Buddhist koan that says: Before enlightenment; chop wood, carry water. After enlightenment; chop wood, carry water.”Now: kept as the chapter's spine, labelled honestly: usually called a koan, but this wording is modern and has no known classical source. Its root is the Chinese layman Pang Yun (740–808), whose verse says his miraculous power was “hauling water and carrying firewood” (a plain rendering of 運水及搬柴).
  • Isha Upanishad epigraph, “Hymns 2-6,” in a modern translation with bracketed edits ([they], [evil], [Self])Now: verse 2 only, word for word from Max Müller's public-domain translation (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1, 1879), as the title-page epigraph.
  • “the Bhagavad Gita is seen as a distillation of the Upanishads and the Upanishads are seen as a distillation of the Vedas”Now: the Gita is a 700-verse poem inside the Mahabharata; an old verse (the Gītā Dhyānam) calls it the milk of the Upanishads; the Upanishads are the philosophical texts that close the Vedas, part of them rather than a separate distillation.
  • Gita 2.47 not quoted in the draftNow: added “Thy right is to work only, but never with its fruits” (Swami Swarupananda's public-domain translation, 1909), because the chapter turns on it. The verse's second half, don't be attached to inaction, is paraphrased and tied to avoidance.
  • Vivekananda's nine-line passage from Karma-Yoga, chapter IV, ending “the highest expression of freedom is to forbear”Now: the first two sentences quoted (“Duty is seldom sweet… a continuous friction otherwise”); the rest paraphrased in one line. Name spelling fixed (draft had “Vivekanada”).

  • “Fortunately, most of the things we avoid due to anxiety are not as awful as war itself, but maybe you are in the military and that is your duty”Now: kept almost word for word, followed by the everyday battlefields (a phone call, an inbox, a hard conversation).   • Krishna, “his charioteer and avatar of the divine”Now: “the divine in human form,” drawn only as a peacock feather at the reins. No likeness of Krishna or Arjuna; Arjuna is the book's small marigold figure.

Illustration language

Smooth lines, meaningful colour, minimal shapes: Japanese print tradition meeting the colours of New Mexico. Every drawing is original; none copies Be Here Now or Hokusai.

  • Brush-pen line: contours swell on the shadow side and taper to fine tips; interior detail is thinner.
  • Matte two-tone shading, light from the top left. No gradients; light is the only glow, plus a faint paper grain inside framed plates.
  • Plates, not icons: each drawing has a setting, depth and a frame when it helps (arch, circle or rounded window).
  • Anatomy and nature drawn true: hearts, lungs, brains, eyes, hands, animals, flowers.
  • One recurring person: the golden seated figure, drawn once and reused, so the reader is always in the picture.
  • New Mexico sunsets, mesas, marigolds and turquoise doors; seigaiha waves, cloud bands and firework chrysanthemums.
Lapis Turquoise Chili Marigold Prickly pear Rust Bone

Before print: rights

Long passages from in-copyright books need permission in a published book, or should become short quotes or paraphrase. That covers Easwaran's Gita and Upanishads, Ram Dass, Sam Harris, Anil Seth, James Nestor, the West Wing scene, Kent Keith's Commandments and Edward de Bono. Vivekananda, Kipling and older Gita translations are public domain. I'm not a lawyer, so check with one before printing.

Grounding · about two minutes · take your time

5

Name five things you can see.

This is 5-4-3-2-1, a grounding exercise. Panic is a loop of thought. Your senses only work in the present, so naming what they find pulls you out of the loop and back into the room. Look around slowly. Say the five things out loud or in your head.

4

Name four things you can touch.

Feel each one for a second before you move on. The chair under you, your feet on the floor, the fabric of your sleeve, the phone in your hand.

3

Name three things you can hear.

Near sounds first, then far ones. Your own breath counts. Notice that the thoughts have to pause while you listen.

2

Name two things you can smell.

Breathe in through your nose to find them. If nothing comes, name two smells you like.

1

Name one thing you can taste.

Even if it's only the inside of your mouth, or the last thing you drank.

Here.

Now breathe out slowly, longer than you breathed in.

Three times. A long out-breath is the body's brake. The alarm is allowed to wind down on its own time. You can run this again whenever the wave starts to build, as often as you need.

If you are in danger or can't keep yourself safe, call or text 9-8-8 (Canada and the US), or 911 in an emergency. This exercise is a tool, not treatment.

Tools

The practices from the book, in one place. The first one is for the moment panic hits.

Not medical advice. If you are in crisis, call or text 9-8-8 (Canada and the US). In an emergency, call 911.

  • Box breathIn 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4. Steady and sharp, for the middle of the day.
  • 4 · 7 · 8In 4, hold 7, out 8. Weighted to the exhale, for winding down.
  • Wizard of AhThree long exhales you can hear.
  • The leversThe Basics on one board. See what neglect does, then pull one.
  • The one with a handleYour breath is the only automatic system you can steer.
  • Leaf on a streamPut each thought on a leaf and let it drift by.
  • Yoga nidraLie down and let a voice walk through the body.

Voices. In edit mode you can record or upload your own voice for each step of 5-4-3-2-1 and the breathing counts. Readers hear you; without a recording they hear a soft chime.
